entries.q: I don't know what help I need. Where do I start?
a: Call 211 or search 211neny.org. 211 is a free, confidential service that connects you to local help with food, housing, utilities, health care and more. It covers Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, and you can call any time, day or night.

For long-term help for older adults or people with any disability (like home care or caregiver support), call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. NY Connects gives free, unbiased information for people of all ages.

To apply online for SNAP (food stamps), HEAP (heating help) and cash assistance, use myBenefits.ny.gov. The site also has a quick check to see what you may qualify for. If you have a housing, food, utility or heating emergency, contact your county Department of Social Services (DSS) right away.
In a life-threatening or medical emergency, call 911.

entries.q: What is the Social Care Network (Healthy Alliance) screening for Medicaid members?
a: New York set up regional Social Care Networks (SCNs) to help Medicaid members with needs like housing, food and transportation. You answer a short set of screening questions, and a navigator can connect you to local programs. Screening and help finding services are free for Medicaid members.

Some members in a Medicaid health plan with certain health needs (like a mental health condition, pregnancy, or a child with asthma) may also get short-term help, such as meals or housing help. It does not change your Medicaid, SNAP or WIC.

Healthy Alliance runs the Social Care Network for the Capital Region, which includes Saratoga County ((518) 520-3211), and the North Country, which includes Warren and Washington Counties ((518) 656-8312).
You can start by answering the state’s screening questions at screening.shinny.org, using Healthy Alliance’s self-screening form, or asking your doctor, care manager or health plan.
The program runs under a federal Medicaid waiver approved through March 31, 2027. New York is asking to extend it, so services may change after that date.

entries.q: What do "income limit" and "Federal Poverty Level" mean?
a: An income limit is the most money your household can have coming in and still qualify for a program. Many programs set their limit as a percent of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL). The FPL is an income amount the federal government sets each year, usually in January.

In 2026, 100% of the FPL is $15,960 a year for one person, $21,640 for two, $27,320 for three and $33,000 for four. Add $5,680 for each extra person. "200% of poverty" means double that amount. For example, 200% for a family of four is $66,000 a year, or $5,500 a month. New amounts are expected in early 2027.

Gross income is your total income before taxes or anything else is taken out. Net income is what is left after the deductions a program allows. For example, SNAP (food stamps) usually checks gross income first, then net income after subtracting things like part of your earnings, child care, high rent and utility costs, and some medical bills for members who are 60 or older or disabled.

Who counts as your "household" depends on the program. For SNAP, it is the people who live together and buy and make meals together. Spouses and most children under 22 who live with you count, even if they eat separately. For health coverage through NY State of Health, your household is usually you, your spouse and the people you claim as dependents on your taxes.
Each program has its own rules, so being a little over a chart does not always mean you are not eligible. The only sure way to know is to apply. Not sure where to start? Call 211.

entries.q: What papers should I bring when I apply for benefits?
a: Bring what you have, but do not wait to apply just because something is missing. For SNAP, the office must accept your application as long as it has your name, address and signature. If you qualify, benefits count from the day you applied.

Most offices ask for: a photo ID; Social Security numbers for each person applying (or proof you applied for one); proof of where you live, like a lease, rent receipt or mail; proof of income, like pay stubs from the last 4 weeks or a benefit award letter; your rent or mortgage bill and your heat, utility and phone bills; and bank statements. Also bring child care receipts, medical bills (for anyone 60 or older or disabled), and a doctor’s statement if someone is disabled, unable to work or pregnant.

If you are not a U.S. citizen, bring your immigration papers. You can apply for your children or other eligible family members even if you are not applying for yourself. For SNAP, the office is not allowed to ask for immigration papers from people who are not applying.

If you are missing a paper, tell the worker. Other kinds of proof often work, like a statement from your landlord or employer. The office will tell you what is still needed and when it is due; for SNAP, you get at least 10 days. Send copies, not originals. Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties have used the free NYDocSubmit phone app for sending papers; ask your DSS.
Warren County DSS posts a full checklist online (warrencountyny.gov/socserv/bring). Washington and Saratoga County DSS can tell you what they need when you call.

entries.q: What's the difference between DSS, OTDA, NY State of Health and Social Security?
a: Your county Department of Social Services (DSS) is where most people apply for and manage SNAP, cash assistance (Temporary Assistance), emergency help, HEAP and child care help. DSS also handles some Medicaid: people on SSI, people who need long-term care at home, the spend-down program, and some people with disabilities.

Local DSS offices: Warren County DSS, 1340 State Route 9, Lake George, (518) 761-6300. Washington County DSS, Municipal Center, Building B, 383 Broadway, Fort Edward, (518) 746-2300. Saratoga County DSS, 152 West High Street, Ballston Spa, (518) 884-4140.

The Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) is the state agency that oversees DSS. You usually do not visit OTDA. It runs myBenefits.ny.gov, the OTDA Hotline (1-800-342-3009), fair hearings when you disagree with DSS, and the state child support program. It also helps decide Social Security disability claims for New Yorkers.

NY State of Health is the state’s official health plan marketplace. Most people under 65 apply there for Medicaid, the Essential Plan, Child Health Plus or a private plan. Many people 65 and older or on Medicare who do not need long-term care now get Medicaid through it too. Call 1-855-355-5777. If you start in the wrong place, staff will help you get to the right one.

Social Security is a federal agency, separate from the state and county. It handles Social Security retirement, SSDI, SSI and Medicare sign-up. Call 1-800-772-1213 or find your nearest office at ssa.gov/locator. Not sure who to call? Dial 211.

entries.q: What is Medicaid, and how do I apply in New York?
a: Medicaid is public health coverage for certain people with low income, including children, families, pregnant people, older adults, and people with disabilities. It pays for a wide range of care. Some services have small co-pays; the state says these can be waived if you cannot afford them.

Most people apply through NY State of Health, online or by calling 1-855-355-5777. This includes adults 19 to 64 without Medicare, children, pregnant people, and parents or caretaker relatives. New York is also moving more people there: people who have both Medicare and Medicaid, people 65 and older who are not asking for long-term care, and many people applying for a Medicare Savings Program.

Some people still apply through their county Department of Social Services (DSS). This includes people who get SSI, people who are blind or disabled and do not fit the groups above, people who need long-term care at home (such as personal care or CDPAP), and people using the spend-down (excess income) program. If you start in the wrong place, staff will help you get to the right one.
Medicaid rules are changing in 2026 and 2027 (see "What Medicaid changes are coming in 2026 and 2027?"). Questions? Call the New York State Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831.

entries.q: What is "straight" (fee-for-service) Medicaid?
a: "Straight" Medicaid, also called fee-for-service, means you are not in a Medicaid health plan. You show your Medicaid card at any doctor, dentist or other provider who is enrolled in New York Medicaid, and Medicaid pays that provider directly.

Some people cannot join a plan, so they stay on straight Medicaid. This includes people on spend-down (excess income), people who have other full health insurance, and people in hospice when they enroll. Some others, such as American Indians and Alaska Natives, may choose not to join a plan.

Even people in a Medicaid plan get some services straight from Medicaid instead of the plan. These are called "carve-outs." For example, since April 2023 people in most Medicaid plans get their prescriptions through NYRx, the Medicaid drug program, and Medicaid rides are set up through the state’s transportation manager. That is one reason to keep your Medicaid card after you join a plan.

Not every provider takes straight Medicaid. Ask the office, "Do you take straight (fee-for-service) Medicaid?" New York also publishes a public list of providers enrolled in Medicaid, but being on the list does not promise they will see you. In this directory, look for the "Straight Medicaid (fee-for-service)" tag.

entries.q: What is a Medicaid managed care plan, and how do I switch plans?
a: Most people with Medicaid must join a Medicaid managed care plan, which is a health plan approved by the state. You do not lose your Medicaid benefits; you get them through the plan.

In a plan, you pick a regular doctor, called a primary care provider (PCP), who helps coordinate your care and refers you to specialists. You usually must use doctors and hospitals in the plan’s network. The plan pays those providers directly.

After you join a plan, you have 90 days to change your mind and switch. After those 90 days, you must stay in the plan for the next nine months, unless you have an urgent reason. Each family member can be in a different plan, and you can change your PCP by calling your plan.
To learn about plans, switch, or ask about an exemption, call New York Medicaid Choice at 1-800-505-5678 (TTY 1-888-329-1541). It is the state’s managed care enrollment program.

entries.q: What Medicaid changes are coming in 2026 and 2027?
a: A 2025 federal law (H.R. 1) is changing some Medicaid rules in New York.

Starting October 1, 2026, some immigrants (such as refugees, asylees, parolees, and survivors of domestic violence or trafficking) may move from Medicaid to the Essential Plan. New York says their benefits will not change. Coverage for children and pregnant people is not changing.

Starting January 1, 2027, some adults ages 19 to 64 will need to show they work, go to school, are in job training, or volunteer. They can meet the rule by earning at least $580 a month, doing 80 hours a month of these activities, or a mix of both. Many people are excused, including people who are pregnant or recently gave birth, people with a disability or a health condition that makes it hard to work, people with Medicare, American Indians and Alaska Natives, and parents or caregivers of a child under 14 or of a person with a disability.

Also starting January 1, 2027, some adults 19 to 64 will need to renew Medicaid every 6 months instead of once a year. And Medicaid will pay fewer past medical bills: 1 month back for adults 19 to 64 and 2 months back for others, instead of 3 months now. Apply as soon as you think you qualify.

What to do now: make sure NY State of Health or your county Department of Social Services has your current address, phone and email, and open every notice you get. Details may change as the state writes its rules.

entries.q: What is a Medicaid spend-down (excess income)?
a: If your monthly income is a little over the Medicaid limit, you may still get Medicaid through the Excess Income program, also called "spend-down" or "surplus income." The amount your income is over the limit works like a monthly deductible. It is for people who are under 21, 65 or older, certified blind or disabled, pregnant, or the parent of a child under 21.

2026 limits for people who are 65 or older, blind or disabled: $1,836 a month for one person and $2,489 for a couple, counted after some deductions (such as $20 of income and most health insurance premiums). Savings must also be under $33,038 for one person or $44,796 for a couple. These limits change each January. Example: if your countable income is $2,000 a month and you live alone, your spend-down is $164 a month ($2,000 minus $1,836). Your caseworker figures the exact amount.

How it works: for doctor visits, prescriptions, home care and other care outside the hospital, send your county Department of Social Services (DSS) medical bills that add up to your spend-down amount. Medicaid then pays your other covered bills for the rest of that month. You do this each month you need care. For hospital care, bills that add up to six months of spend-down get you six months of coverage.

Bills that count can be paid or unpaid: doctors, dentists, clinics, eye exams, lab tests, prescriptions, rides to medical care, home health aides, medical supplies, hearing aids, glasses, and co-pays and deductibles (including Medicare). The provider does not have to take Medicaid for the bill to count, but once you meet your spend-down, Medicaid only pays providers enrolled in Medicaid. Bills for your spouse and your children under 21 count too. Old unpaid bills that a provider is still trying to collect can count, and so can bills you paid in the 3 months before the month you applied (including what EPIC paid).

No bills this month? You can pay your spend-down amount to your county DSS instead (the "Pay-In" option); only do this in months you need care. Make appointments and fill prescriptions early in the month. If a disability makes it hard to get to the DSS office, you have the right to fax your bills in instead; ask your caseworker.

If you are disabled (at any age, including 65 and older), a pooled income trust can end the monthly spend-down. See "How can a pooled income trust end my Medicaid spend-down?" Questions: call your county DSS or the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831.

entries.q: How can a pooled income trust end my Medicaid spend-down, and how do I set one up?
a: A pooled income trust is run by a nonprofit. Each month you deposit your spend-down amount into your own account in the trust. Medicaid does not count that money, so you get full Medicaid with no spend-down. The trust then uses your money to pay your bills, such as rent, utilities, food and clothing. Many people use one to get Medicaid home care and stay in their own home.

Who can use one: people with a disability as Social Security defines it, at any age. If you get SSDI or SSI because of a disability, you usually already qualify. If you are 65 or older without that, Medicaid must decide that you are disabled first: your county DSS gathers your medical records and sends them to the state’s Disability Review Unit. A Medicare card alone does not prove a disability.

How to set one up: 1) Pick a trust and fill out its enrollment papers, called a joinder agreement. 2) Attach the papers the trust asks for. 3) Make the first deposit and pay any fees. For example, NYSARC Trust Services (Community Trust II, (518) 439-8323) has listed a $300 first deposit that includes a one-time $200 enrollment fee, plus a monthly fee based on your deposit. Ask the trust for its current fees.

Then tell Medicaid: give your county DSS a copy of the trust papers and a written statement of how much income you will deposit each month, and ask that your Medicaid be figured with no spend-down. If you need a disability decision, ask for it at the same time. After that, deposit your spend-down amount every month and send the trust the bills you want paid.

Things to know: check your next Medicaid notice to make sure the spend-down is gone. If you stop depositing, the spend-down comes back. Fees come out of your deposits. Cash the trust gives you directly counts as income, so trusts pay your bills for you. Money left in the account when you die may stay with the trust or pay Medicaid back. If you are 65 or older, putting savings (not monthly income) into a pooled trust can lead to a penalty if you later need nursing home Medicaid, so get advice first.

NYSARC is one of several nonprofit pooled trusts in New York, and fees and services differ, so it’s worth comparing. The paperwork can be confusing: a free legal aid office (see the Legal Help category) or the Medicaid Helpline, 1-800-541-2831, can help.

entries.q: What is Health Home care management?
a: A Health Home is not a building. It is a group of health and service providers that work together for you. Once you enroll, you get a care manager who works with you on a care plan. Joining is your choice, and you can leave at any time.
A care manager can help connect you to doctors, mental health and substance use care, medicines, housing, and services like food, benefits and transportation.

To qualify, you must have Medicaid and either two or more chronic conditions (such as asthma or diabetes) or one of these: HIV/AIDS, serious mental illness (adults), sickle cell disease, or serious emotional disturbance or complex trauma (children). A substance use disorder alone does not qualify, but it counts as one of two conditions. You must also need this level of care management.

To enroll, ask your Medicaid plan, doctor, hospital, discharge planner, or county Department of Social Services, or contact a Health Home directly. In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, the state lists Adirondack Health Institute (adults and children) and Children’s Health Home of Upstate New York (children); Saratoga County also has Central New York Health Home Network.

entries.q: Can Medicaid give me a ride to a medical appointment?
a: Yes. Medicaid members can get free non-emergency rides to and from Medicaid-covered medical appointments, such as the doctor or the dentist. Rides are not given to pharmacies, gyms, schools or grocery stores. For an emergency, call 911.

In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, rides are arranged by Medical Answering Services (MAS). Call the upstate line at 1-866-932-7740 or set up an account on the MAS website. This is the same whether you have straight Medicaid or a Medicaid plan.
Call at least 72 hours (3 days) before your appointment. Every trip must be approved ahead of time. Rides for urgent sick visits can sometimes be set up sooner.

The ride type depends on your needs. It can be a bus, taxi, ambulette, or money back for mileage if you or someone you know drives you. Taxis and ambulettes need a form from your medical provider. Rides are usually to the nearest provider who can meet your needs.

entries.q: What is Managed Long Term Care (MLTC)?
a: Managed Long Term Care is for people with Medicaid who are chronically ill or disabled and want to stay at home. A long-term care plan covers services like home health aides, personal care, nursing at home, therapy at home, adult day health care, and CDPAP.
There are three kinds: MLTC partial capitation plans (age 18 and up, with Medicaid), Medicaid Advantage Plus plans (age 18 and up, with both Medicaid and Medicare), and PACE (age 55 and up).

To join an MLTC or Medicaid Advantage Plus plan, you must be assessed as needing these services for more than 120 days. Since September 1, 2025, new members must also meet the state’s "minimum needs" rule: needing at least limited hands-on help with more than two daily activities (like bathing or dressing), or, with dementia or Alzheimer’s, needing supervision with more than one. People already in a plan before then keep the old rules if they stay enrolled. PACE has its own rules.
The assessment is done by the New York Independent Assessor Program (see the NYIA question). Then New York Medicaid Choice helps you pick a plan.

entries.q: What is CDPAP, and can a family member be paid to care for me?
a: CDPAP (Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program) is a Medicaid program that lets people who qualify for home care choose and hire their own caregiver, called a personal assistant.
The assistant can be a friend or family member, but not your spouse, your designated representative, or (for someone under 21) a parent.

To qualify, you need Medicaid, a stable medical condition, and an assessment showing you need home care. Adults 21 and older who are newly assessed on or after September 1, 2025 must also meet the state’s minimum needs rule; people already getting services before then keep the old rules. You must be able to direct your own care, or have a designated representative who can.
Since 2025, every CDPAP member must use one statewide company, Public Partnership LLC (PPL), to handle the assistant’s payroll.

entries.q: What is the NYIA (New York Independent Assessor) assessment?
a: Before Medicaid approves personal care, CDPAP, or a Managed Long Term Care plan, you need an assessment from the New York Independent Assessor Program (NYIAP). It is for adults 18 and older with Medicaid, and it is run for the state by a company called Maximus.

There are two parts: a Community Health Assessment done by a registered nurse, and a clinical exam by an independent doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant who does not already treat you. Visits can be in person or by video. People who may need more than 12 hours of care a day on average also get a review by an Independent Review Panel. Have your medical records ready.

To schedule, call the NYIAP Helpline at 1-855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541). Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30 AM to 8 PM, and Saturday, 10 AM to 6 PM, closed state holidays. You will get the results by mail.

sections.title: Health insurance words and medical bills

entries.q: What do insurance words like premium, deductible, copay and coinsurance mean?
a: A premium is what you pay to have insurance, usually each month, even if you never see a doctor. A deductible is the amount you pay for covered care each year before your plan starts to pay its share. Many plans pay for some care, like a yearly checkup, before you meet the deductible.

A copay (copayment) is a set dollar amount you pay for a visit or a prescription, like $25. Coinsurance is a percent of the cost you pay after you meet your deductible. For example, with 20% coinsurance you pay $20 of a $100 visit, and the plan pays $80.

The out-of-pocket maximum (or limit) is the most you have to pay for covered, in-network care in a plan year. After you reach it, the plan pays the full cost of covered in-network care for the rest of the year. It does not include your monthly premiums, care your plan does not cover, or most out-of-network care.

A network is the group of doctors, hospitals and other providers your plan has a contract with. In-network care costs you less. Out-of-network care usually costs more, and some plans do not pay for it at all except in an emergency (see the question on surprise bills).

Prior authorization (also called preauthorization or prior approval) means your plan must agree a service or medicine is needed before it will pay. An approval is not a promise to pay, and you do not need one to get emergency care. A referral is a written order from your main doctor to see a specialist; many plans, especially HMOs, require one. Before a big test or a specialist visit, call the number on your insurance card and ask: Is this provider in my network? Do I need a referral or prior authorization?

entries.q: How do I keep my Medicaid? What happens at renewal?
a: Medicaid does not continue forever on its own. You must renew it (also called recertifying) to keep it. Most people renew once a year. Starting in 2027, most adults ages 19 to 64 will renew every 6 months instead. Children, people with disabilities, and American Indian and Alaska Native adults will still renew once a year. If you apply before January 1, 2027, or renew before March 1, 2027, you get 12 months first (see the question on Medicaid changes).

If you signed up through NY State of Health, the state first tries to renew you on its own, using information it already has. You may not need to do anything. If it needs more, it will send you a notice asking you to log in to your NY State of Health account and send information. To find your renewal date, log in at nystateofhealth.ny.gov and click the "Plans" tab.

If your Medicaid is handled by your county Department of Social Services (DSS), for example if you get SSI, are on spend-down, or get long-term care at home, your county handles your renewal. Watch your mail, send back the renewal form by the date on it, and call your county DSS with questions. The office that handles your case can change, for example when you turn 65 or get Medicare, so read each letter to see who to answer.

Open every letter, text and email from NY State of Health, your county or your health plan, and answer by the date it gives. The state sends a warning at least 15 days before coverage ends. Keep your address, phone and email up to date so notices reach you.

If your Medicaid ends because you did not send in your renewal or information, you usually have 90 days to send it and be reviewed without starting a new application. If you think Medicaid was ended by mistake, you can ask for a fair hearing (see that question). For help, call NY State of Health at 1-855-355-5777 (TTY 1-800-662-1220), call the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831, or meet with a free enrollment assistor.

entries.q: I can't pay my hospital bill. Can I get help?
a: Yes. Every New York hospital licensed by the Department of Health must offer financial assistance (sometimes called charity care). All of them must use the same form, the NYS Uniform Hospital Financial Assistance Application. Ask the hospital's billing or financial aid office for it. The hospital must tell you about financial aid in writing when you register and when you leave.

You may qualify if you have no insurance, if your insurance benefits have run out, or if you have insurance but paid more than 10% of your income on medical costs in the last 12 months. People with household income up to 400% of the federal poverty level are eligible. Below 200%, the hospital must waive all charges; between 200% and 400%, you pay a reduced amount on a sliding scale that the law caps. Only income counts, not your house, car or savings. Immigration status does not matter. For non-emergency care, you may need to live in the hospital's service area, and the hospital may ask you to apply for Medicaid or the Essential Plan first.

You can apply at any time, even after the bill goes to collections. You do not have to pay while your application is being decided. Payment plans can't be more than 5% of your monthly income, and interest is capped at 2%. A hospital can't refuse medically necessary care because of an unpaid bill, and it can't sue patients under 400% of the poverty level. This law covers hospital bills, not separate bills from doctors who are not hospital employees.

New York also protects people with medical debt. Hospitals and health care providers can't put a lien on your main home or garnish your wages for medical debt, and medical debt is not allowed on your credit report. Be careful: if you pay a medical bill with a regular credit card, it is no longer medical debt and you lose these protections. A provider can't require you to put a credit card on file before you get needed or emergency care.

For free help applying or appealing a denial, call Community Health Advocates at 1-888-614-5400 (Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.). To report a hospital breaking the financial aid rules, email HFAL@health.ny.gov. For problems with medical debt or credit cards, call the Attorney General's helpline at 1-800-771-7755.

entries.q: I got a surprise bill from a doctor or hospital outside my network. What can I do?
a: A surprise bill is a bill from an out-of-network provider that you did not choose, often after emergency care or a hospital stay. Both federal law (the No Surprises Act) and New York law protect you. If you have Medicaid or Medicare, you already have separate protection from these bills; call your plan if you get one.

For emergency care, and for care from an out-of-network doctor at an in-network hospital or surgery center, you usually only have to pay what you would pay in-network: your normal copay, coinsurance or deductible. Billing you for more than that (called balance billing) is not allowed. Federal law also covers air ambulance bills. Ground ambulance bills are not covered by the federal law, but New York law gives some protection, so call DFS if you get one.

In New York, it can also be a surprise bill if your in-network doctor sent you to an out-of-network provider or lab and you did not sign a paper saying you knew they were out-of-network. For this kind of bill, you must send a Surprise Medical Bill Certification Form to your health plan and the provider. The form is on the NY Department of Financial Services (DFS) website.

If you have no insurance or are paying for care yourself, providers must give you a Good Faith Estimate of the cost before scheduled care, or when you ask. If your bill is at least $400 more than the estimate, you can dispute it within 120 days of the date on the bill.

What to do: don't ignore the bill, but don't pay the extra amount yet. Call your health plan and the provider and say you believe it is a surprise bill. For help, call DFS at 1-800-342-3736, the Attorney General's Health Care Helpline at 1-800-428-9071, or the federal No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 (open 7 days a week).

entries.q: Does Medicaid cover dentures, glasses and hearing aids?
a: Yes. New York Medicaid covers medically necessary dental, eye and hearing care, both with straight Medicaid and in Medicaid health plans. You must use a provider who takes Medicaid. Some items need prior approval (permission from Medicaid first); your provider asks for it for you.

Teeth: Medicaid covers exams, cleanings, X-rays, fillings, pulling teeth, root canals, crowns and dentures. Since January 2024, more crowns and root canals are covered to help you keep your own teeth. Implants, including a single implant, can be covered when your dentist shows they are medically necessary and other choices like dentures won't work. Dentures, even if lost or broken, are usually replaced only once every 8 years, unless your dentist shows a new set is medically necessary.

Eyes: Medicaid covers eye exams and glasses, usually one exam for glasses and new lenses every two years. You can get them sooner for some conditions, like diabetes, glaucoma, a fast-changing cataract, or a child's quickly changing eyesight. Lost or broken glasses can be replaced. Contact lenses are covered only when medically necessary.

Hearing: With a referral from a doctor, physician assistant or nurse practitioner, Medicaid covers hearing tests. It also covers hearing aids, ear molds, batteries and repairs when testing shows you need them. Adults 21 and older need prior approval for two hearing aids. A lost, stolen or broken hearing aid can be replaced if it is out of warranty. Medicaid does not pay for FM systems, listening devices or tinnitus maskers.

Small copays may apply. A Medicaid dentist can't charge you more than the copay unless you agree and sign a private-pay agreement before treatment starts. To find a provider who takes Medicaid, call your health plan or the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831, or search this directory for "Straight Medicaid".

entries.q: Can I see a doctor if I don't have insurance?
a: Yes. Community health centers, also called Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), are clinics that get federal funding and must serve everyone, even people who can't pay. They offer medical, dental, mental health and substance use care. Many have on-site pharmacies with discounted medicines, and many can help with rides.

Health centers adjust what you pay based on your income and family size. This is called a sliding fee scale. Under federal rules, people with income at or below the poverty level get a full discount or pay only a small set fee, and people with income up to twice the poverty level get a partial discount. If you have insurance but can't afford your deductible or copays, ask the health center if its sliding fee can help.

In this area, Hudson Headwaters Health Network is an FQHC with many health centers. Its Sliding Fee Program lowers the cost of medical and dental care, X-rays and many prescriptions. You can apply whether or not you have insurance. Ask at any Hudson Headwaters health center or call its Sliding Fee Program at (518) 824-8640.

To find other health centers, use the federal Find a Health Center tool at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov. Also check whether you qualify for free or low-cost coverage like Medicaid or the Essential Plan (see those questions), and ask any hospital about financial assistance.

entries.q: My pharmacy says my medicine isn't covered. What can I do?
a: A generic drug has the same active ingredient as the brand-name drug and works the same way, but usually costs less. A formulary (drug list) is the list of medicines a plan covers. Some drugs need prior authorization, which means your prescriber must get the plan's OK first.

If you have Medicaid, your medicines are covered by NYRx, New York's Medicaid drug program. Since April 1, 2023, this includes people in Medicaid managed care plans, HARPs and HIV Special Needs Plans. This change did not include long-term care plans (like MLTC, MAP or PACE) or the Essential Plan; if you are in one of those, ask your plan how your medicines are covered. To find a pharmacy that takes NYRx, use the pharmacy locator on the state's NYRx page or ask your pharmacy.

NYRx copays are $1 for generics and preferred brands, $3 for non-preferred brands, and 50 cents for over-the-counter medicine. There is no copay for people under 21, during pregnancy and for about two months after, people with income below the poverty level, nursing home residents, or for mental health medicines and birth control, among others. There is also a yearly limit on copays. A pharmacy can't refuse to give you your medicine because you can't pay the copay.

If the pharmacy says a drug isn't covered, ask why. Often it needs prior authorization, or a "preferred" drug on the list would work. Ask your doctor to request approval from Medicaid or switch you to a preferred drug. If the pharmacist can't reach your doctor, the pharmacist can get approval to give you up to a 72-hour emergency supply. Questions: Medicaid Helpline, 1-800-541-2831.

If you have a Medicare drug plan (Part D), you, your doctor or someone acting for you can ask the plan for a "coverage determination." This includes an "exception" to cover a drug not on the plan's list or to skip a rule like prior authorization. Your doctor must send a statement explaining why you need that drug. If the plan says no, you can appeal. For help with drug costs, see the questions on Extra Help and EPIC.

entries.q: Can immigrants get Medicaid or the Essential Plan in New York?
a: It depends on immigration status, age, income, and whether you are pregnant. Some rules changed in 2026 because of a federal law (H.R. 1). Apply or ask before you decide you can't get coverage.

Children under 19 can get Child Health Plus no matter their immigration status, if they otherwise qualify. Pregnant people can get full Medicaid no matter their immigration status, with coverage for 12 months after the pregnancy ends. NY State of Health says coverage for children, pregnant people and people who recently gave birth is not changing.

Starting October 1, 2026, some immigrants, including refugees, asylees, parolees, and survivors of domestic violence or human trafficking, may move from Medicaid to the Essential Plan. Their benefits are not supposed to change. Since July 1, 2026, DACA recipients with income over 138% of the poverty level no longer qualify for the Essential Plan. Some lawfully present immigrants who get tax credits may see cost changes starting in 2027.

Undocumented adults ages 19 to 64 can usually get only Emergency Medicaid, if they meet the income rules. Emergency Medicaid pays to treat an emergency medical condition, including labor and delivery. Since 2024, undocumented adults 65 and older may qualify for full Medicaid in New York, paid with state funds. To get it, you first apply for Emergency Medicaid at your county Department of Social Services.

To apply, call NY State of Health at 1-855-355-5777 or meet with a free enrollment assistor. Not sure where to apply? Call the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831. If you are worried about your immigration case, see the question on public charge. A free legal aid office or the NY Office for New Americans hotline (1-800-566-7636) can help with your situation.

entries.q: Will using Medicaid or other benefits hurt my green card application ("public charge")?
a: Public charge is a test immigration officers use when some people apply for a green card (permanent residence). Officers look at your age, health, family, money and skills to decide if you are likely to depend on the government in the future.

The rules changed on September 18, 2026, for green card applications filed on or after that date. Officers may now consider most income-based benefits, such as Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, that you apply for, are approved for, or get on or after that date. Getting a benefit does not by itself mean you will be denied; it is one part of the whole picture. Benefits you got before September 18, 2026 are judged under the older rule, which only counted cash assistance and long-term care in an institution paid by the government. Earned benefits like Social Security, Medicare and unemployment insurance are not counted.

Many people are not affected. The test is part of a green card application, not a citizenship application, and it usually does not apply to people who already have a green card. Refugees, asylees, people applying for TPS, VAWA self-petitioners, T and U visa holders, and special immigrant juveniles are exempt. Being pregnant does not make you exempt.

Benefits your family members get, like a U.S. citizen child's Medicaid, are not counted as your own benefits. But if a family member gets benefits because your income is low, officers may consider your low income.

These rules are new and could change. Before you drop or turn down health coverage or food help, get advice. Call the New York State Office for New Americans hotline at 1-800-566-7636 (free, anonymous, many languages; Monday to Friday 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., weekends 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) to be connected with free immigration legal help.

entries.q: What is the Essential Plan?
a: The Essential Plan is low-cost health insurance from NY State of Health for adults 19 to 64 who live in New York, are lawfully present, and are not eligible for Medicaid, Child Health Plus, or job-based or other coverage.

It has a $0 monthly premium and no deductible. It covers dental and vision, hospital care, prescriptions, and free preventive care. Some members with higher incomes pay small copays for some visits and medicines. You can enroll any time of year.

Income limits changed on July 1, 2026. For 2026, the most you can make is $31,920 for one person, $43,280 for two, $54,640 for three, and $66,000 for four. These amounts usually change each year. People who earned a bit more (between 200% and 250% of the poverty level) lost the Essential Plan and may be able to buy a Qualified Health Plan with financial help instead.
Apply online at NY State of Health, call 1-855-355-5777 (TTY 1-800-662-1220), or get free help from a certified enrollment assistor.

entries.q: What is Child Health Plus?
a: Child Health Plus is New York's health insurance for children under 19 who live in New York and don't have other health insurance. Depending on family income, a child may get Children's Medicaid or Child Health Plus. Children can get Child Health Plus no matter their immigration status.

entries.q: Can I get VA health care as a veteran?
a: You may be eligible for VA health care if you served in the active military, naval or air service and did not get a dishonorable discharge.

If you enlisted after September 7, 1980, or entered active duty after October 16, 1981, you generally must have served 24 months in a row or the full period you were called to, with some exceptions (for example, a discharge for a service-related disability).

Under the PACT Act, VA has expanded health care to veterans exposed to toxins or other hazards while serving, at home or abroad. This includes all veterans who served in the Vietnam War, Gulf War, Iraq, Afghanistan, or any other combat zone after 9/11, if they meet the basic service and discharge rules.

Some things place you in a higher priority group, which makes you more likely to get care. These include a service-connected disability, a VA pension, or getting (or qualifying for) Medicaid. If none apply, you may still qualify based on income.

If you have an other than honorable discharge, you may still get some care, such as emergency mental health care if you are in crisis, and you can ask for a discharge upgrade. Apply online at VA.gov or call 1-877-222-8387 (Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern).

entries.q: Who can get Medicare, and when does it start?
a: Medicare is federal health insurance for people 65 or older who meet citizenship or residency rules. Some people under 65 can get it earlier because of a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD, permanent kidney failure), or ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease).

Age 65: if you already get Social Security retirement or disability benefits before you turn 65, you usually get Medicare automatically. If not, you sign up through Social Security. Premium-free Part A usually starts the month you turn 65.

Disability: Social Security automatically enrolls you in Medicare Parts A and B after you have received disability benefits (SSDI) for 2 years. SSDI itself usually starts after a 5-month waiting period, so this is often about 2 and a half years after your disability began. With ALS, Medicare generally starts the first month you are eligible for disability benefits.

ESRD: if you are on dialysis, Medicare usually starts on the first day of the fourth month of dialysis, at any age, if you (or your spouse or parent) meet the work history rules. It can start sooner if you do home dialysis training or get a kidney transplant. To apply, call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213.
SSI by itself does not qualify you for Medicare.

entries.q: What are Medicare Parts A, B, C and D?
a: Part A (hospital insurance) helps cover hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care, hospice, and some home health care.

Part B (medical insurance) helps cover doctors and other providers, outpatient care, medical equipment like wheelchairs and walkers, and many preventive services like screenings and shots. Part B has a monthly premium.

Part C is Medicare Advantage: a private plan approved by Medicare that bundles Parts A and B, and usually D. You may need to use the plan's network and get approval before some care. Most plans add extras like some vision, hearing and dental care.
Part D helps pay for prescription drugs. You get it from a private drug plan added to Original Medicare, or through a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage.
Original Medicare is Parts A and B. Medigap (Medicare Supplement Insurance) is extra insurance you can buy to help pay what Original Medicare does not, like the 20% coinsurance.

entries.q: When can I sign up for Medicare or change my Medicare plan?
a: Initial Enrollment Period: 7 months around your 65th birthday. It starts 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ends 3 months after it. Signing up late can mean a late penalty added to your premium, usually for as long as you have that coverage.

General Enrollment Period: January 1 to March 31 each year, if you missed your first chance. Coverage starts the month after you sign up. A Special Enrollment Period may let you sign up later without a penalty, for example within 8 months after job-based coverage or the job ends. COBRA and retiree coverage do not count for this.
Open Enrollment: October 15 to December 7 each year. You can join, switch or drop a Medicare Advantage or drug plan. Changes start January 1.
Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment: January 1 to March 31. If you are already in a Medicare Advantage plan, you can switch to another one or go back to Original Medicare (and join a drug plan).

If you have Medicaid or get Extra Help, you may be able to change your drug coverage once a month. Other life changes, like moving, can also open a Special Enrollment Period. Free help: HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501.

entries.q: What is a Medicare Savings Program (QMB, SLMB, QI)?
a: A Medicare Savings Program (MSP) uses Medicaid to help people with limited income pay Medicare costs. Every MSP in New York pays the Part B premium, so it is no longer taken out of your Social Security check.

In New York there are two levels. QMB (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary) also pays Part A premiums if you have them, plus Medicare deductibles and coinsurance. With QMB, Medicare providers are not allowed to bill you for Medicare-covered care, except for a small Medicaid co-pay; show your Medicare and Medicaid (or QMB) cards each visit. QI (Qualifying Individual) pays the Part B premium only, and you can't have QI and Medicaid at the same time.

For 2026 in New York, QMB is for incomes at or below $1,836 a month for one person ($2,489 for a couple). QI is for incomes below $2,474 a month ($3,355 for a couple). entries.q: What is Extra Help (the Part D Low-Income Subsidy)?
a: Extra Help is a Medicare program that helps people with limited income and resources pay for Medicare drug coverage (Part D): premiums, deductibles and co-pays. While you have it, you also do not pay a Part D late penalty.

You get Extra Help automatically if you have full Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program, or SSI. Otherwise, you can apply through Social Security any time, online or at 1-800-772-1213. For 2026, the limits are about $23,940 a year in income and $18,090 in resources for one person (higher for couples). These limits change each year, and a free HIICAP counselor (1-800-701-0501) can help you apply.

With Extra Help, drug co-pays are low. In 2026, Medicare says people with Extra Help pay no more than $12.65 for each covered drug. Starting January 2027, Medicare lists up to $5.80 for each generic drug and $14.40 for each brand-name drug, and $0 once your yearly drug costs reach the Part D limit. Many plans have a $0 premium with Extra Help.
If you have Medicaid or get Extra Help, you may be able to change your drug plan once a month.

entries.q: What is EPIC?

entries.q: Should I choose Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare with a Medigap plan?
a: With Original Medicare (Parts A and B), you can see any doctor or hospital in the U.S. that takes Medicare, usually without referrals or prior approval. But you usually pay 20% coinsurance for Part B services, with no yearly limit. Many people add a Medigap policy (Medicare Supplement Insurance) to help pay those costs, plus a separate Part D plan for drugs.

Medicare Advantage (Part C) is a private plan that you use instead of Original Medicare. Most include drug coverage, and many add extras like some dental, vision or hearing care. Each plan has a yearly limit on what you pay for covered services. But you usually must use the plan's network, and you may need referrals and prior approval for some care. You can't use a Medigap policy with Medicare Advantage.

The trade-off in short: Medicare Advantage puts everything in one plan with a yearly cost limit, but gives you less choice of doctors and more approvals. Original Medicare plus Medigap gives you more choice and fewer approvals, but you pay a premium for the Medigap policy and the drug plan on top of Part B.

New York gives you extra protection. If you have Parts A and B, you can buy a Medigap policy at any time of year, and the company generally can't turn you down or charge more because of your health or age. This includes people under 65 who have Medicare because of a disability. A policy can make you wait up to 6 months for coverage of a health problem you already had, but that wait is shortened or dropped if you had other coverage with no gap of more than 63 days.

You can change Medicare plans from October 15 to December 7 each year, with changes starting January 1. If you are in Medicare Advantage, you can also switch plans or go back to Original Medicare from January 1 to March 31. Before you decide, call HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501 or your county Office for the Aging for free counseling (see the question on help choosing a Medicare plan).

entries.q: What is hospital "observation status," and why does it matter for rehab in a nursing home?
a: In the hospital, you are either an inpatient or an outpatient. You are an inpatient only after a doctor writes an order to admit you. If you are "under observation," you are an outpatient, even if you stay overnight in a regular hospital bed.

This affects what you pay. As an outpatient, you usually pay a copay for each hospital service under Part B, and the pills you normally take at home may not be covered. It matters even more if you need rehab afterward. In most cases, Original Medicare pays for a skilled nursing facility only after an inpatient stay of at least 3 days in a row. Time under observation or in the emergency room does not count.

If you are under observation for more than 24 hours, the hospital must give you a Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice (MOON). It tells you that you are an outpatient and why. Ask your doctor each day, "Am I an inpatient or under observation?" If you may need rehab, ask whether you should be admitted.

If you were admitted as an inpatient and the hospital later changed you to observation, you may have the right to a fast appeal. This right started February 14, 2025, for people in Original Medicare. You should get a Medicare Change of Status Notice before you leave; if you don't, ask for it. Appeal to the Quality Improvement Organization (BFCC-QIO) named on the notice, ideally while you are still in the hospital.
Medicare Advantage plans may have different rules, and some waive the 3-day stay. For help, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), or see the question on free help choosing a Medicare plan (HIICAP).

entries.q: I have both Medicare and Medicaid. Which one pays, and what plans can I join?
a: People with both Medicare and full Medicaid are called "dual eligible." Medicare pays first for Medicare-covered care. Medicaid pays after that, and covers things Medicare doesn't, like long-term care at home or in a nursing home. Medicaid may also pay your Medicare premiums, deductibles and coinsurance (see the Medicare Savings Program question).
Your prescriptions are mostly covered by a Medicare drug plan (Part D), not by Medicaid, though Medicaid may still cover some drugs Medicare doesn't. You automatically get Extra Help with drug costs.

You can keep Original Medicare and straight Medicaid, or join a plan that puts both together. New York has three kinds of these integrated plans. Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP) is for adults 18 and older who need long-term care for more than 120 days. PACE is for people 55 and older who need long-term care, with a care team and a day center; it is not offered in every area. IB-Dual is for people who don't need long-term care: you keep your Medicaid health plan and join the same company's Medicare plan for dual eligibles, called a D-SNP.

If you are in a Medicaid health plan when you become eligible for Medicare, your plan may sign you up for its D-SNP automatically. It must send you a notice at least 60 days before. You can say no, but then you may have to leave that Medicaid plan and go to regular (fee-for-service) Medicaid. In these plans you usually must use the plan's doctors.

Free help choosing: HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501, New York Medicaid Choice at 1-888-401-6582 (for MAP and PACE), or Medicare at 1-800-633-4227. If you have a problem with a plan, ICAN (the Independent Consumer Advocacy Network) gives free help at 1-844-614-8800.

sections.title: Social Security, SSI and disability income

entries.q: What is the difference between SSI, SSDI and Social Security retirement?
a: SSI (Supplemental Security Income) is for people who are 65 or older, blind, or disabled AND have very little income and few resources (things you own). It does not depend on your work history. In New York, people who get SSI also get Medicaid without a separate application.

SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance) is for people with a disability who have worked and paid Social Security taxes long enough. For most adults that means about 5 of the last 10 years; younger workers may need less. The amount depends on your past earnings. After 2 years on SSDI, you get Medicare (sooner for ALS and kidney failure).
Social Security retirement can start as early as age 62 if you worked and paid Social Security taxes for about 10 years or more. Medicare is separate and generally starts at 65.
Many people get both SSI and Social Security benefits. It is possible to have both Medicare and Medicaid. If you have SSI and Medicare, you automatically get Extra Help with drug costs.
To apply or ask questions, call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.

entries.q: Who can get SSI, and how much does it pay?
a: SSI pays monthly benefits to adults and children who are blind, have a disability, or are 65 or older, and who have little or no income and resources.
Resources are things you own, like money in the bank. The limit is $2,000 for one person or $3,000 for a couple. Your home, one car used for transportation, and household goods do not count.

For 2026, the most the federal government pays is $994 a month for one person and $1,491 for an eligible couple. Other income lowers the payment. New York adds a small State Supplement (SSP), which depends on your living situation. In New York, people who get SSI also get Medicaid. These amounts change each January; 2027 amounts are announced in October 2026.

To apply, adults can start an SSI application online at ssa.gov/apply/ssi, or call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) to set up a phone or in-person appointment. Once you get SSI, you must report your wages every month, and report changes in other income, what you own, and where or with whom you live.

entries.q: How does SSDI work, and how long is the wait?
a: SSDI pays monthly benefits to people with a disability or blindness that keeps them from working for a year or more, or is expected to result in death, and who have enough work history.
If you are working, your earnings must be below a limit called "substantial gainful activity" (SGA). In 2026, that is $1,690 a month ($2,830 if you are blind). The limit changes each January.
There is a 5-month waiting period. Benefits generally start in the sixth full month after the date Social Security decides your disability began. There is no waiting period for ALS.
Medicare starts automatically after you have received SSDI for 2 years (sooner for ALS and kidney failure). Part A is free; Part B has a monthly premium.
You may be able to go back to work, or keep working, without losing your SSDI benefits right away. Ask Social Security about the work rules before you start a job, and report any work.

entries.q: When can I start Social Security retirement benefits?
a: You can start retirement benefits as early as age 62 if you worked and paid Social Security taxes for about 10 years or more (40 work credits).

If you start before your full retirement age, your monthly check is reduced a little for each month you start early. For people born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67, and starting at 62 lowers the check by about 30%.
If you wait past full retirement age, up to age 70, your monthly benefit goes up (about 8% for each full year you wait).

Medicare is separate. Most people sign up for Medicare Parts A and B when they are first eligible, usually at age 65. Even if you wait to start Social Security, sign up for Medicare around your 65th birthday, or it may cost more later.

entries.q: What is a representative payee?
a: A representative payee is a person or organization that Social Security picks to receive and manage Social Security or SSI payments for someone who cannot manage their own money.

Social Security usually looks for family or friends first. If none can do it, it looks for a qualified organization. While you are able to, you can also name up to three people ahead of time who could be your payee if you ever need one ("advance designation").

The payee must use the money for the person's needs. All payees must keep records of how the money is spent or saved, and many must file a yearly report. Parents and spouses who live with the person usually do not have to file the yearly report, but they still must keep records.
If you are worried someone cannot manage their benefits, call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) to ask for an appointment.

entries.q: What is an ABLE account?
a: An ABLE account is a tax-advantaged savings account for a person with a disability. The money can pay for disability-related costs like housing, transportation, health care, education and basic living expenses.

Starting January 1, 2026, the disability must have begun before age 46 (it used to be age 26). People on SSI or SSDI because of a disability that started before 46 can qualify, and others can qualify with a signed disability certification.

For SSI, the first $100,000 in an ABLE account does not count toward the $2,000 resource limit. If the balance goes over that, SSI checks may pause, but Medicaid continues. When the owner dies, money left in the account may have to pay back Medicaid.

Anyone can put money in. The yearly limit for all deposits together is $20,000 in 2026 (it can change each year). Some people who work can add more from their own pay. A person can have only one ABLE account.

entries.q: Can I work while I get SSI or SSDI?
a: Yes. Social Security has "work incentives," rules that let you try working without losing all your benefits at once. Always report your work and your pay to Social Security.

SSI: Social Security does not count $20 of your income and the first $65 you earn each month, and it counts only half of your earnings above that. So your SSI check goes down about $1 for every $2 you earn. In 2026, students under 22 can have up to $2,410 a month of earnings not counted (up to $9,730 a year). Some costs you pay because of your disability so you can work can also be subtracted. If your check stops because of your pay, you can often keep Medicaid, and SSI can restart without a new application if your pay drops.

SSDI: you get a Trial Work Period of 9 months (within a rolling 5 years) when you keep your full check no matter how much you earn. In 2026, any month you earn over $1,210 counts as a trial month. After that comes a 36-month period when you get your check for any month you earn less than "substantial gainful activity" (SGA). In 2026, SGA is $1,690 a month, or $2,830 if you are blind. These amounts change each January.

If your benefits stop because of work and your condition later keeps you from working, you can ask for Expedited Reinstatement within 5 years. You can get up to 6 months of temporary payments while Social Security decides.

Free help: Ticket to Work offers free job services to people 18 to 64 on SSI or SSDI. Free benefits counseling (WIPA) explains how a job will affect your benefits before you take it. Call the Ticket to Work Help Line at 1-866-968-7842 (TTY 1-866-833-2967). Also ask your county DSS about New York's Medicaid Buy-In for working people with disabilities.

entries.q: I got a Social Security overpayment letter. What can I do?
a: An overpayment means Social Security says it paid you more than it should have. The letter says why and how much. Read it right away, because the first 30 days matter.

If you think the amount is wrong, or that you were not overpaid at all, file an appeal called a "reconsideration" (form SSA-561). You have 60 days after you get the letter. If you appeal within 30 days, Social Security will not collect until it decides.

If the amount is right but it was not your fault and you cannot afford to pay it back (or it would be unfair), ask for a waiver with form SSA-632. You can upload it through your my Social Security account, or mail or fax it to your local office. You can ask for a waiver at any time, but if you ask within 30 days, Social Security will not collect until it decides. If the overpayment is $1,000 or less, you may be able to ask by phone.

If you do nothing, Social Security will start keeping part of your check until it is paid back: for most Social Security overpayment letters sent since April 25, 2025, up to 50% of your monthly benefit; for SSI, 10% of the payment. Your letter gives your rate. To pay less each month, send form SSA-634. To pay or set up a payment plan, call 1-855-807-8807, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. local time. If you no longer get benefits, the money can be taken from tax refunds or wages.
A free legal aid office can help with your situation. You can also call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). Keep copies of everything you send.

entries.q: How can I save money and still keep SSI or Medicaid?
a: SSI has a resource limit: $2,000 for one person or $3,000 for a couple. Resources are things like cash, bank accounts, stocks and savings bonds. If what you own is over the limit at the start of a month, you get no SSI for that month.

Many things do not count: your home, household goods, one car used for transportation, burial spaces, up to $1,500 each in burial funds for you and your spouse, and life insurance with a total face value of $1,500 or less. Back payments from SSI or Social Security do not count for 9 months. Tax refunds, including the EITC, do not count for 12 months.
An ABLE account lets some people with disabilities save up to $100,000 without it counting for SSI. See "What is an ABLE account?" for who qualifies.

Trusts: a supplemental (special) needs trust for a disabled person under 65, or a pooled trust run by a nonprofit, generally does not count for SSI or Medicaid if it is set up correctly. Special rules can apply to people 65 and older. When the person dies, money left in the trust may have to pay Medicaid back. Money the trust pays to you directly counts as income. For SSI, trust payments for rent or housing can lower your check (by up to $351.33 a month in 2026), but payments for things like phone bills or medical care do not.

Pooled trusts and spend-down: in New York, a person who is certified disabled, at any age, can put their extra (excess) income into a pooled trust each month. Medicaid then does not count that income, which can end the monthly spend-down. The trust pays the person's bills, such as rent and utilities, from that money. Give your county DSS a copy of the trust and a written statement of how much you will deposit each month. Rules differ for some married people in long-term care plans. Talk to a lawyer before setting up any trust; a free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What tax credits can put money in my pocket, even if I don't owe taxes?
a: Some tax credits are "refundable." That means if the credit is more than the tax you owe, you get the rest back as a refund. You must file a tax return to get them, even if you don't owe any taxes.

The federal Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) is for people who work and earn low to moderate pay. For tax year 2025 (the returns filed in 2026), it is worth up to $649 with no children, $4,328 with one child, $7,152 with two, and $8,046 with three or more. Income limits depend on family size. For example, a single parent with one child could earn up to $50,434. New York State has its own earned income credit (generally 30% of the federal credit) that adds to the federal one.

The federal Child Tax Credit is worth up to $2,200 for each child under 17 for tax year 2025. Up to $1,700 per child can come back as a refund if you earned at least $2,500. You (or your spouse, if filing jointly) and each child need a Social Security number that is valid for work.

New York's Empire State Child Credit is also refundable. It is for full-year New York residents with a child under 17. For tax year 2025, it is up to $1,000 for each child under 4 and $330 for each child age 4 to 16. For tax year 2026 (filed in 2027), the amount for ages 4 to 16 goes up to $500. Amounts are smaller at higher incomes. See the next question for free help filing.

File online for free: if your 2025 income (adjusted gross income) was $89,000 or less, you can use IRS Free File software. Each company may have its own rules, so check before you start to avoid a fee. Free File Fillable Forms are free at any income if you are comfortable doing your own return. New York's Taxpayer Assistance Program (TAP) also offers free guided help, in person or online, for people with income of $89,000 or less. entries.q: How do I get unemployment benefits in New York?
a: Unemployment Insurance (UI) pays weekly benefits to people who lost their job or had their hours cut, and who are ready, willing and able to work. You need enough recent wages from work. For claims starting in 2026, you generally need at least $3,500 in wages in your best calendar quarter (a 3-month period), plus wages in at least one other quarter. If you quit or were fired, apply anyway. The Department of Labor (DOL) will review your claim.

File in your first week out of work, because waiting can cost you benefits. Apply online at unemployment.labor.ny.gov (best between 7:30 a.m. and 7:30 p.m.). Or call the Telephone Claim Center at 1-888-209-8124, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Interpreters are available by phone. The first week is an unpaid waiting week. The first payment usually comes 2 to 3 weeks after your claim is processed.

How much and how long: your weekly amount is based on your past wages. As of late 2025, the most anyone could get was $869 a week; this can change each October. You can get up to 26 weeks of benefits. To estimate your amount, use the DOL Benefit Rate Calculator.

"Certifying" means asking for each week's payment. You must do it every week you are out of work. Weeks run Monday to Sunday. Certify for the past week any time from that Sunday through the next Saturday, online or by phone at 1-888-581-5812. Report any work you did, even if it was only an hour. You must also do at least 3 work search activities each week, or follow an official work search plan.
If you are denied, you have 30 days from the date of the decision to ask for a hearing.

entries.q: How do I get or change child support in New York?
a: Your county's child support office can help you get a support order from Family Court. Once there is an order, the Support Collection Unit collects payments from the other parent, keeps track of them, and sends them to you.

To start, enroll online at childsupport.ny.gov, or get a paper enrollment form from your local child support office. If you apply for cash assistance, you are referred automatically, and Medicaid applicants may be too. If working on child support would go against your child's best interests, for example because of safety, tell the worker. A cash assistance applicant can refuse without penalty in that case.

Family Court figures support using a set guideline: a percent of the parents' combined income after certain deductions (17% for one child, 25% for two, 29% for three, 31% for four and at least 35% for five or more), plus each parent's share of child care, medical and school costs. A $35 yearly fee is taken from payments only for parents who never got cash assistance, after $550 in support is collected in a year (October to September).

Changing an order: only a court can change it, so keep paying the full amount until it does. Either parent can ask Family Court for a change (Form 4-11) if there is a big change in circumstances. Being in jail or prison does not stop you from asking. For orders from October 13, 2010 or later, you can also ask if 3 years have passed or if either parent's gross income changed by 15% or more (a drop in income counts only if it was not your choice). Every 2 years the program also checks orders for a cost-of-living increase.
Questions? Call the Child Support Helpline at 888-208-4485 (TTY 866-875-9975), Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What is SNAP (food stamps), and what are the work rules?
a: SNAP gives monthly benefits on an EBT card to buy food at approved stores. It helps low-income working people, older adults, people with disabilities and others. Eligibility depends on household size, income and other factors, and most households do not have a savings (resource) test.

From October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027, the most a household can get is $306 a month for one person and $1,023 for four people. Most households get less. These amounts change every October. Apply at myBenefits.ny.gov or at your county Department of Social Services. OTDA Hotline: 1-800-342-3009.

Work rules: adults 18 to 64 who are able to work and do not live with a child under 14 (called ABAWDs) can get SNAP for only 3 months in 3 years, unless they work, train or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. Many people are excused, for example people 65 or older, households with a child under 14, people who are pregnant, people who get disability benefits, and people who cannot work 80 hours a month because of a physical or mental health reason.

New York's 3-year clock for this time limit started over on October 1, 2026 (the new period runs to September 30, 2029). If you lost SNAP because of the work rules before then, you can reapply, or ask to be added back to your household's case. Call your county DSS if you think you should be excused.
Tip: you can freeze your EBT card when you are not using it to help protect your benefits from theft.

entries.q: What is WIC?
a: WIC (Women, Infants, and Children) is a free nutrition program. It gives money for healthy food and infant formula, plus pregnancy and breastfeeding support.

entries.q: What is Temporary Assistance (cash assistance), and what about emergencies?
a: Temporary Assistance (TA), also called Public Assistance, is cash help for people who cannot work, cannot find a job, or do not earn enough. It is run by your county Department of Social Services.

Family Assistance is for families with a minor child living with a parent or caretaker relative. Adults have a lifetime limit of 60 months. Safety Net Assistance is for people who do not qualify for Family Assistance; cash Safety Net is generally limited to 2 years in a lifetime, and after that help comes in non-cash form, such as payments made directly to a landlord or utility. There are exceptions, so ask DSS about your situation.

Emergency Assistance can help with an urgent need, like being homeless, having little or no food, an eviction notice, a utility shut-off notice, no heating fuel in cold weather, or violence or threats from a partner or household member. You do not need to be on ongoing TA to get emergency help.
If you have an emergency, contact your county DSS as soon as possible and tell them it is an emergency. You should be interviewed and told the decision in writing the same day you apply.

entries.q: What is HEAP (help with heating bills)?
a: The Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) helps eligible New Yorkers heat and cool their homes. You may qualify if your household income is under the limit, or if you get SNAP, Temporary Assistance, or SSI as a person living alone (Code A).

Regular HEAP gives one benefit per season. For 2026-2027, it is scheduled to open November 2, 2026. The 2026-2027 base benefit is $990 (plus add-ons) for households that buy oil, kerosene or propane, and $400 (plus add-ons) for electric or gas heat. Amounts and dates change each season.

Emergency HEAP (for 2026-2027, scheduled to open January 4, 2027) helps if your heat or electricity is shut off or about to be, or you are almost out of fuel. Call your county HEAP contact for an emergency.

Homeowners may also get help to repair or replace a broken furnace or boiler (up to $4,000 to repair, $8,000 to replace), and some can get a yearly "clean and tune" (up to $500). Money for these is limited and the rules can change each year; last season, repair and replacement was only for homeowners 60 or older. Ask your county HEAP contact what is open now and who qualifies.
Apply at myBenefits.ny.gov or your county DSS. OTDA Hotline: 1-800-342-3009. The 2026-2027 income limits are on the OTDA HEAP page.

entries.q: What is the difference between LIHEAP, HEAP and weatherization?
a: LIHEAP is the federal program that funds help with home energy costs. It does not give grants directly to people, and it never charges a fee for a benefit. If someone offers you a "LIHEAP grant" or asks for a fee, it is a scam. To get help with heating bills in New York, apply for HEAP (see the HEAP question).

HEAP helps pay heating bills, fuel and energy emergencies. Weatherization is different: it makes your home more energy efficient, so it costs less to heat and stays safer over time. Work can include sealing air leaks, insulation, and heating system repairs.

In New York, your household is usually automatically eligible for weatherization if someone in your home gets SSI, Public Assistance, or HEAP. Otherwise, you may qualify if your household income is at or below 60% of the state median income.

Homeowners and renters pay nothing for weatherization services; owners of rental buildings must pay part of the cost. Priority goes to older adults, families with children, and people with disabilities. To apply, contact your local provider and ask if funds are available now. On the state's March 2026 list: Warren and Washington counties, Warren-Hamilton Counties Action Committee for Economic Opportunity, (518) 793-0636; Saratoga County, LifeWorks Community Action, (518) 288-3206 ext. 115. The state weatherization office is at (518) 474-5700.

entries.q: What is Lifeline (discount phone or internet)?
a: Lifeline is a federal program that gives a monthly discount on phone, internet, or bundled service from participating companies. The discount is up to $9.25 a month for internet or bundled service, or up to $5.25 for phone-only service (more on Tribal lands).

You qualify if your household income is at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, or if someone in your home gets SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal public housing assistance (including Section 8), or a Veterans Pension or Survivors Benefit.
Only one Lifeline benefit is allowed per household. You must recertify every year. If your service is free, use it at least once every 30 days or it may be turned off.

Apply online through the National Verifier at lifelinesupport.org, by mail, or through a phone or internet company. For help or a paper form, call 1-800-234-9473. Survivors of domestic violence or human trafficking who ask their cell phone company to separate their line from an abuser's plan may get emergency Lifeline support for up to six months.
New York also requires larger internet companies to offer $15 or $20 monthly plans to households on SNAP, Medicaid or some other programs. Ask your internet company.

entries.q: Can I get help paying for child care?
a: Yes. New York's Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP), often called the child care subsidy, helps families on Temporary Assistance and other low-income families pay for child care so parents can work or become self-sufficient.

entries.q: What can I do if DSS denies or cuts my benefits? (Fair hearings)
a: If you think a decision your county Department of Social Services made about your case is wrong, you can ask for a fair hearing. An Administrative Law Judge from the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) hears your side and issues a written decision. The decision can order the county to fix your case.

You can request a hearing online, by phone at 1-800-342-3334, by mail, or by fax (518-473-6735). Don't wait: for cash assistance, Medicaid and HEAP you usually have 60 days from the notice, and for SNAP 90 days. Some notices give less time, so check the deadline on your notice.

If the county plans to cut or stop a benefit, send your request in the way and by the date described in your notice (before the change takes effect). This protects your right to "aid continuing," which can keep your benefits the same until the hearing decision. If you lose the hearing, you may have to pay back benefits you got while waiting.

If you win and the county does not do what the decision says, you can file a compliance complaint with OTDA. Free legal help may be available from the Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York: 1-833-628-0087.

entries.q: How do SNAP interviews and renewals work, and what if my EBT benefits are stolen?
a: After you apply for SNAP, you must do an eligibility interview, by phone or in person. You should get a decision within 30 days. If you have little or no money, ask to be checked for "expedited" (fast) SNAP. If you qualify, you get your first benefits within 7 days.

Renewing (recertification): about two months before your benefits end, you get a packet in the mail with a form and a phone interview time. Send in the form before the interview date, at myBenefits.ny.gov or by mail, fax or in person. You can also ask for a face-to-face interview. If your form arrives after the interview date, it is up to you to reschedule before your benefits end.

Reporting changes: your notice tells you what to report. Under New York's usual rules, you must report if your household's total monthly income before taxes goes over the limit on your notice. Report it within 10 days after the end of that month. If you are approved for more than 6 months, you may also get a Periodic Report form partway through. Return it by the due date on the form, or your SNAP may stop. If you don't report, you may have to pay benefits back.

Stolen benefits: thieves can copy EBT cards with hidden "skimmers" on card readers, or trick you with fake texts and calls. Stolen SNAP benefits can no longer be replaced. Stolen cash assistance (TA) may be replaced once per federal year (October to September) if you apply within 30 days of finding the theft. Either way, call EBT Customer Service at 1-888-328-6399 right away for a new card.

Protect your card: use the ebtEDGE app or ebtEDGE.com to freeze your card between uses, change your PIN often, and block out-of-state and online purchases. Never give your PIN to anyone who calls or texts you.
