entries.q: Can my power or heat be shut off? What protections do I have in New York?
a: New York's Home Energy Fair Practices Act (HEFPA) protects people with electric or gas service at home. Before a shutoff, your utility must send a written final notice and wait 15 days so you can pay or make a payment plan. Shutoffs can only happen Monday to Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. They are not allowed on holidays, the day before a holiday, or the two weeks around Christmas and New Year's. You have a right to pay overdue bills in reasonable installments based on what you can afford (a "deferred payment agreement").

Medical emergency: if someone in your home has a serious illness or condition that a shutoff would make worse, get a certificate from a doctor or the local board of health. Your service may not be shut off while it is in effect. After 30 days the doctor must renew it, and you must show you cannot pay. If the service runs life-support equipment, the certificate stays in effect, but every 3 months you must show why you cannot pay.

Older, blind or disabled: tell your utility if you are 62 or older, blind or disabled, and everyone else at home is 62 or older, 18 or younger, blind or disabled. The utility must then make special efforts to reach you before and after a shutoff. From November 1 to April 15, utilities must also make a special effort to find out if turning off heat would seriously harm anyone's health or safety.

Energy Affordability Program (EAP): large electric and gas utilities give a monthly bill discount to lower-income customers. If you get HEAP, you should get the discount automatically. People who get SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, TANF or some other benefits, or who have lower income, may also qualify. If you think you qualify but don't see the discount, call your utility.

If you get a shutoff notice, call your utility first to set up a payment plan. If that doesn't work, call the Department of Public Service emergency hotline at 1-800-342-3355 (business days, 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.). For other utility complaints, call 1-800-342-3377. Also ask your county DSS about Emergency HEAP and emergency assistance.

entries.q: Is there help paying for a funeral or burial?
a: Low-income families may get help paying for a burial from their county Department of Social Services (DSS). Each county sets its own steps and limits, and DSS will count money the person left, insurance, and what responsible relatives can pay. The state Attorney General says you can apply up to 120 days after the death, but call DSS as soon as you can, and before you sign a funeral contract if possible. Warren County DSS: 518-761-6300. Washington: 518-746-2300. Saratoga: 518-884-4140.

Social Security pays a one-time $255 death payment to a surviving spouse, or if there is no spouse, to some children. Family members may also get monthly survivor benefits. Funeral homes usually tell Social Security about the death. Call 1-800-772-1213.

Veterans: burial in a VA national cemetery is free for eligible veterans. It includes the gravesite, opening and closing the grave, a liner, a headstone or marker, and ongoing care of the grave. The VA may also pay a burial allowance if the veteran meets VA rules. For a death not caused by military service on or after October 1, 2026, it is up to $1,032 for burial and $1,032 for a plot. For a service-connected death on or after September 11, 2001, it is up to $2,000. These amounts usually change each October. Apply at VA.gov.

Your rights: a funeral home must give you an itemized price list (called a General Price List) when you ask. You do not have to buy a casket or urn from the funeral home, and it cannot charge you extra for one bought somewhere else.

entries.q: What is the difference between Section 8 and public housing, and how do waiting lists work?
a: A Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher helps pay rent in a private apartment or house that you find. The housing agency pays part of the rent straight to the landlord. You usually pay about 30% of your adjusted monthly income (your income after certain deductions). If the place you first rent costs more than the agency's limit, your share can go up to 40%. You can sometimes move with your voucher; ask the agency about its rules first.
Public housing is apartments or homes owned and run by a local housing authority. Your rent is usually based on 30% of your adjusted income, with a small minimum rent.

Both are for low-income households, including older adults and people with disabilities. You apply with your local housing agency. Demand is high, so you will usually go on a waiting list, and some lists close. You can apply to more than one waiting list. An agency cannot require you to live in its area to apply, but some give preference to local residents, and you may have to rent in that area at first.

For Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) lists JEM Inc. in Saratoga Springs, (518) 372-8846, as its local Section 8 administrator. When HCR waiting lists are open, you can apply online through the MyHousing Portal (section8.hcr.ny.gov), or on paper with the local administrator. Applying is free. Never pay anyone who says they can get you on a list or move you up.
While you wait, keep the housing agency up to date on your address, phone and household size. An agency can remove you from the list if you don't answer its letters.

entries.q: What does "homeless" mean for housing programs (HUD categories)?
a: HUD-funded homeless programs use four categories.

Category 1, literally homeless: sleeping in a place not meant for people to live (like a car or outside); staying in a shelter, transitional housing, or a motel paid for by a charity or government program; or leaving an institution (like a hospital or jail) after 90 days or less, if you were homeless right before you went in.
Category 2, imminent risk: you will lose your home within 14 days, you have no other place lined up, and you don't have the money or people to help you get housing.

Category 3 covers some youth under 25, and families with children, who count as homeless under other federal laws. Few HUD programs use it. Category 4 covers people fleeing or trying to flee domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, stalking or human trafficking, who have no other safe place to live and no resources to get one.
Which category you are in can affect which programs you qualify for. Each program may have extra rules. Tell the worker exactly where you slept last night and how long you have been there.

entries.q: What is coordinated entry for homeless services?
a: Coordinated entry is the way a community (called a Continuum of Care) decides who gets referred to housing programs for people who are homeless. It is required for programs that get certain HUD homeless funding.
There are four steps: access (where you first connect), assessment (questions about your situation and needs), prioritization, and referral to housing and services.

Because there is not enough housing for everyone, people with the most serious needs and risks are usually prioritized first. Things that can raise priority include serious health problems, frequent use of emergency rooms, jails or psychiatric hospitals, and sleeping outside. Each community sets its own priority rules.

Coordinated entry should never stop anyone from getting emergency shelter. Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties (along with Hamilton County) are served by the Saratoga-North Country Continuum of Care. Its plan names each county's Department of Social Services (DSS) as the first referral for emergency shelter and housing, and many local agencies can connect you. Start with your county DSS, or call 211 for help.

entries.q: How does an eviction work in New York, and what should I do at each step?
a: In New York, a landlord must go to court to evict you. Only a sheriff, marshal or constable can remove you, and only with a court order called a warrant of eviction. Changing the locks, shutting off your electric or water, taking your things, or keeping you out without that order is an illegal eviction, and it is a crime. If it happens, call the police, then call a free legal aid office.

In a case about unpaid rent, the landlord should first send a late notice by certified mail if rent is more than 5 days late. Then the landlord must give you a written 14-day rent demand. If you do not pay within those 14 days, the landlord can start a court case. The court papers (a notice of petition and a petition) must be delivered 10 to 17 days before the court date. If the landlord just wants to end or not renew your tenancy, the landlord must give you 30, 60 or 90 days' written notice, depending on how long you have lived there.

Do not ignore court papers. If you do not go to court, you can lose the case without being heard. At your first court date, you can ask the judge to postpone (adjourn) the case, for example to get a lawyer, and the next date will be at least 14 days later. Bring your lease, rent receipts, letters, and photos of any repair problems. Problems like needed repairs can be a defense.

If the landlord wins, the judge signs a warrant of eviction. A sheriff, marshal or constable must then give you a written notice at least 14 days before the eviction, and evictions happen only on business days, in daylight. In a case about unpaid rent, paying everything you owe before the eviction is carried out should stop it. If you get a 14-day notice, act right away. To ask the court for more time or to stop the eviction, you usually need to file papers called an order to show cause. The court clerk or a legal aid office can help.

Get free help as early as you can. Outside New York City, apply online through EvictionDefenderNY on LawHelpNY, or call the Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York at (833) 628-0087. Its Saratoga Springs office serves Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties. For help paying back rent, ask your county Department of Social Services (DSS) about emergency assistance, or call 211. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What are my basic rights as a renter in New York (deposits, repairs, Section 8)?
a: Security deposit: a landlord cannot ask for more than one month's rent as a deposit, and cannot ask for last month's rent on top of it. After you move out, the landlord has 14 days to return the deposit, or to give you an itemized list of what was taken out for damage. If the landlord does not send that list within 14 days, they must return the whole deposit. You can ask the landlord to inspect before you move out, so you have a chance to fix problems. (Rent-regulated apartments have different deposit rules.)

Other money rules: before you sign a lease, the most a landlord can charge for a credit and background check is $20, and they must give you a copy. Rent is not late until it is more than 5 days past due, and a late fee can be no more than $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less.

Repairs: every lease includes a promise that your home will be livable, safe and clean. This is called the "warranty of habitability." Examples of problems are no heat or hot water, or bugs that are not taken care of. Tell the landlord in writing, keep a copy, and take photos. You can also report problems to your local housing or code enforcement office. Be careful about holding back rent: the landlord can sue you for it, although a judge may lower the rent if the landlord did not make repairs. In most rentals, it is illegal for a landlord to punish you, for example by trying to evict you, for a good-faith complaint. (This rule does not cover owner-occupied buildings with fewer than 4 units.)

Section 8 and other income: in New York, a landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because you pay with a Section 8 voucher, public assistance, Social Security, child support or any other lawful source of income. This is called source-of-income discrimination. A few small rentals where the owner lives, like a room in the owner's home or a two-family house, may be exempt.

To report discrimination, contact the NYS Division of Human Rights at (844) 697-3471 or use its online form. It is free and you do not need a lawyer. For discrimination on or after February 15, 2024, you have 3 years to report it. For security deposit problems, call the NY Attorney General's office at 1-800-771-7755.

entries.q: How do I ask my landlord for a change because of a disability?
a: If you have a disability, federal and New York law say a housing provider must make reasonable changes so you can use and enjoy your home. A "reasonable accommodation" is a change to a rule, policy or service. A "reasonable modification" is a physical change to your home or a shared area.

Examples of accommodations: an assigned parking space near your door when parking is usually first-come; an assistance animal in a "no pets" building; letting a friend mail your rent if your disability makes it hard to leave home; or, in a voucher program, extra time to find a unit or an extra bedroom for a live-in aide. The landlord cannot charge you an extra fee or deposit for an accommodation.

Examples of modifications: grab bars in the bathroom, a ramp at the entrance, wider doorways, or lever door handles. In most private housing, the landlord must allow the change but you pay for it, and you may have to put the inside of the unit back when you move out. In public housing and other federally funded housing, the housing provider usually pays, unless the cost would be an undue burden.

How to ask: you can ask out loud, but it is best to ask in writing and keep a copy. Say that you have a disability, what change you need, and how it helps. If your disability is not obvious, the landlord may ask for reliable proof that you have a disability and need the change. A letter from a doctor or other medical professional, a peer support group, a service agency, or another reliable third party can work.

If you are turned down, ask why, and whether another change would meet your need. You can file a free complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights at (844) 697-3471. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: I have nowhere to sleep tonight. What do I do?
a: Contact your county Department of Social Services (DSS) as soon as you can. If you are homeless, DSS can give emergency help, including paying for a shelter or a motel stay. You do not have to already get Temporary Assistance (cash assistance) to get emergency help. DSS should interview you and tell you its decision in writing the same day you apply.

After business hours, on weekends and on holidays, each county keeps an emergency number for DSS. Some counties, like Warren County, have it answered by the sheriff's office. Check the DSS listing for your county in this directory for the after-hours number, or call 211.

In winter, New York has "Code Blue" rules. When the temperature, with wind chill, is expected to drop below 32 degrees for at least 2 hours in a row, the county must call a Code Blue and take emergency steps to get people who are homeless out of the cold. A Code Blue should last until it warms above 32 degrees, and at least until 7 a.m. the next morning. Our directory lists local Code Blue shelters.

211 Northeast NY covers Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties. Dial 2-1-1, or (888) 366-3211, to find shelter and other help. If you are in danger, call 911. If you are fleeing abuse, call a 24-hour domestic violence hotline (in the crisis bar at the top of this site). They can help you get to a safe place, and they keep shelter locations private for safety.

entries.q: How do I get an order of protection, and what if it is broken?
a: An order of protection is a court order that tells someone to stop hurting, threatening or harassing you. A judge can order the person to stay away from you and your children, to move out, to give up guns, or not to harm pets. A New York order is good anywhere in the state, and it can be enforced in other states too.

Family Court is for people who are "family or household members": a current or former spouse, someone you have a child with, a relative by blood or marriage, or someone you have or had an intimate relationship with, even if you never lived together. You file a family offense petition at your county's Family Court. It is free to file. You have the right to a lawyer in Family Court, and the court will assign one if you cannot afford one.

Criminal court can give an order of protection only when the person has been charged with a crime, for example after an arrest. The district attorney asks the judge for it. Family Court is your own civil case; in criminal court the State, through the district attorney, brings the charges. You can have both kinds of orders at the same time.

Family Court may give you a temporary order the same day you ask. It usually lasts until the next court date, and it can be extended. If Family Court is closed (nights, weekends or holidays), a local criminal court, such as a town or city court, can give a temporary order; then go to Family Court when it opens. An order only works after it has been served (formally delivered) to the other person. A final Family Court order usually lasts up to 2 years, or up to 5 years in serious cases, and the judge can extend it.

If the person breaks the order, call 911. Breaking an order of protection is a crime. You can also file a violation petition in Family Court. Keep a copy of your order with you. Once you have a final order, you can ask for a free Hope Card, a wallet-size or digital copy that police will enforce. For help any time, call the NYS Domestic and Sexual Violence Hotline at 1-800-942-6906, or text 844-997-2121.

entries.q: I am being abused at home. What is a safety plan, and what other protections are there?
a: A safety plan is your own plan to stay safer and be ready if you are in danger. It can include a code word to tell friends you need help, copies of important papers kept where you can get them, a bag packed with clothes, money and medicine for you and your children, a safe place to go, and ways to protect your phone and internet use. A domestic violence advocate can help you make one. If you are in danger now, call 911.

You can call the NYS Domestic and Sexual Violence Hotline any time at 1-800-942-6906, or text 844-997-2121. Conversations are confidential. Warren and Washington Counties and Saratoga County also have 24-hour local hotlines, listed in the crisis bar at the top of this site. These programs can help you find a safe place to stay. For safety, we never list where shelters are.

New York's Address Confidentiality Program (ACP) is free. It gives you a substitute mailing address in Albany to use instead of your real address, and forwards your mail to you. It is for victims of domestic violence, sexual offenses, human trafficking, stalking and kidnapping who have moved or are moving for safety. People in your household can join too. An application assistant, often at a domestic violence program, can help you apply. ACP toll-free phone: (855) 350-4595.

Ending a lease early: under New York law (Real Property Law 227-c), if you or someone in your household is a victim of domestic violence and fears more violence by staying, you can end your lease. Give the landlord written notice at least 30 days before you plan to leave. Within 25 days of the notice, give proof, such as an order of protection, a police report, a medical record, or a signed statement from someone like a domestic violence advocate. The landlord must keep this private.

The Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York has a domestic violence legal program that serves Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties: call (833) 628-0087. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: How can I use this site safely if someone checks my phone or computer?

entries.q: Can I get help paying costs after I was the victim of a crime?
a: Yes, you may. The NYS Office of Victim Services (OVS) can pay back some out-of-pocket costs caused by a crime that happened in New York. This is called crime victim compensation. Not every victim qualifies for every kind of help. Usually you must have been physically hurt, but some people qualify without an injury, such as children, people 60 or older, people with disabilities, and victims of some crimes like stalking. OVS pays last, after other sources like health insurance or workers' compensation.

OVS can help with: medical and counseling costs; lost wages or lost support, up to $30,000; funeral and burial, up to $12,000; moving and storage, up to $2,500; repairing or replacing essential personal property, up to $2,500; crime scene cleanup, up to $2,500; rides to crime-related medical appointments and court; and domestic violence shelter costs.

Rules changed on December 31, 2025. You now have 3 years to file a claim, and OVS can accept a late claim for a good reason, such as not knowing the program existed. Instead of a police report, a victim service program, or a medical or mental health provider who is helping you, can fill out an OVS Crime Verification Form. OVS can decide your claim even if no one was arrested or convicted.

To apply, use OVS Compass online or a paper application from ovs.ny.gov. You do not need a lawyer or a Social Security number. A local victim assistance program can help you apply. In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, the Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York's Crime Victims Attorney Project gives free civil legal help to crime victims at any income: (833) 628-0087. Call OVS at 1-800-247-8035, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

entries.q: How do I get a free lawyer for a problem that isn't a criminal case?
a: Civil legal aid is free help from a lawyer for problems that are not criminal charges. Legal aid offices often help with eviction and housing, homelessness prevention and foreclosure, public benefits like SNAP or disability, family matters like orders of protection, problems for older adults, and some consumer and tax problems.

Free legal aid is mostly for people with low income. The Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York (LASNNY) says your household income should generally be at or below 200% of the federal poverty level (about twice the poverty line). Some of its projects have higher income limits or none at all.

In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, LASNNY has an office in Saratoga Springs. Call (833) 628-0087 toll-free or (518) 587-5188 (Relay 711). Phone intake goes on each day until the schedule fills, so call early. Emergencies, like a court date within 5 business days, no utilities, or a domestic violence safety issue, are taken even if the schedule is full. If LASNNY can't take your case, it may refer you to a volunteer private lawyer who helps for free with some problems, such as divorce, bankruptcy, wills and consumer debt.

LawHelpNY.org has a free directory of legal help by county, plain-language guides and forms, and a LiveHelp chat (Monday to Thursday, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.). If you are facing eviction outside New York City, apply through EvictionDefenderNY on LawHelpNY.

entries.q: What is the difference between guardianship, a power of attorney and a health care proxy?
a: All three let someone else make decisions for a person. The big differences are who picks the helper, what decisions they cover, and whether a court is involved.

A power of attorney (POA) is a paper you sign to name an "agent" to handle your money and property, like banking, bills, benefits and taxes. You choose the agent. It does not cover medical decisions. You must be at least 18 and able to understand what you are signing. In New York it must be signed in front of a notary and two witnesses (the notary can be one of them). A health care proxy is a separate form that names someone to make medical decisions only if you cannot. Many people need both. (See our entry on health care proxies and MOLST.)

Guardianship is when a judge appoints someone to make decisions for a person who can no longer manage. It takes a court case, and the judge may pick someone the person would not have chosen. A POA and health care proxy only work if they are signed while the person can still understand them. Planning ahead can often avoid guardianship.

New York has two kinds of adult guardianship. Article 81 (Mental Hygiene Law) can be used for any adult who cannot manage personal needs or property. The court looks at what the person can and cannot do, not just a diagnosis. A court evaluator looks into the case, there is a hearing, and the judge gives the guardian only the powers that are needed. It is meant to be a last resort.

Article 17-A (Surrogate's Court Procedure Act) is for adults with an intellectual or developmental disability. It is filed in Surrogate's Court. The courts call it the most restrictive kind of guardianship in New York, because it covers most decisions a parent makes for a child. Less restrictive choices include a power of attorney, a health care proxy, and supported decision-making, where a person picks trusted helpers but still makes their own decisions. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What is Clean Slate, and will my old criminal record be sealed?
a: Clean Slate is a New York law that seals many old criminal convictions automatically, so you do not have to apply. It took effect November 16, 2024. The court system has up to 3 years from that date, until November 2027, to set up the process and seal records that already qualify. So many eligible records are not sealed yet.

A misdemeanor can be sealed 3 years after sentencing, or after release if you were in jail. A felony can be sealed 8 years after sentencing or release from prison. You must have no new convictions, no pending charges, and be off probation or parole. A new conviction, or having probation or parole revoked, restarts the clock. Sex offenses, murder and other non-drug Class A felonies are not sealed.

Sealed records are hidden from most background checks for jobs and housing. You do not have to report a sealed conviction on license applications to the NYS Department of State, but until a conviction is actually sealed, you must still report it when asked. Police, courts and prosecutors can still see sealed records. So can some other checks, such as fingerprint background checks required by law, jobs with children, older adults or other vulnerable people, gun licenses, commercial driver's licenses and public housing.

To see your NYS record, ask the Division of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) for a Record Review. You get fingerprinted through IdentoGo, (877) 472-6915. The fee is $17.50 for New York residents (as of February 2026), and you can ask for a fee waiver. Until the courts finish Clean Slate sealing, your record will still show convictions that will be sealed later. A free legal aid office can tell you if you can ask a court to seal a record sooner.

entries.q: How do I replace a lost birth certificate or Social Security card?
a: Birth certificate: if you were born in New York State outside New York City, you can order a certified copy from the NYS Department of Health (DOH) Vital Records, or from the local registrar where you were born. The local registrar is usually the city, town or village clerk. If you were born in New York City, DOH does not have your record; order from the NYC Health Department instead.

You can order your own birth certificate, or your child's if your name is on it. Others need a New York State court order. DOH charges $45 online or by phone (plus a vendor fee), or $30 by mail. DOH says it has long delays right now. Local registrars also give copies; call ahead for their fee, hours and what to bring. DOH Vital Records: (855) 322-1022.

You need a copy of photo ID, such as a driver's license, NYS non-driver ID, passport or U.S. military ID. If you do not have photo ID, DOH accepts two papers that show your name and address, such as a utility or phone bill, or a letter from a government agency dated in the last six months.

Social Security card: a replacement is free. Often you do not need the card at all, just the number. Start online at ssa.gov; you may be able to finish there. If not, you will need an appointment at a Social Security office. The office cannot print a card for you; it comes in the mail 5 to 10 business days after your request is finished. Call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) for help.

entries.q: A debt collector is calling, or I got sued over a debt. What are my rights?
a: A debt collector must give you written "validation" information in its first message or within 5 days. It must name who you owe, break down the amount (interest, fees, payments and credits), and give a date by which you can dispute the debt, about 30 days. If you dispute in writing by that date, the collector must stop collecting the disputed amount until it sends proof.

Old debts: in New York, a collector generally has 3 years to sue you over consumer credit debt, like a credit card or loan. After that, they cannot sue you or threaten to sue. Making a payment after the 3 years are up does not restart the clock.

Some income is protected ("exempt") from debt collectors, including Social Security, SSI, public assistance, veterans' benefits, unemployment, workers' compensation, child support and pensions. If federal benefits like Social Security or SSI are directly deposited, your bank must leave you two months' worth even if a collector tries to freeze your account. New York also protects a set amount in most bank accounts; LawHelpNY lists the current amounts, which change from time to time. If your account is frozen, tell the bank and the collector in writing that the money is exempt (LawHelpNY has sample letters), and get legal help right away.

If you are sued, do not ignore the court papers. Respond by the deadline on the papers. Answering does not mean you admit you owe; it makes the collector prove the debt. If you do not answer, the court can give the collector a "default judgment." Then the collector may be able to take part of your pay (garnish wages) or freeze your bank account, and a judgment is hard to undo.

For free help, call the Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York at (833) 628-0087. To complain about a debt collector, call the NY Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Someone says they can get me benefits, a grant or money if I pay a fee first. Is it a scam?
a: Be very careful. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says offers of free government grant money are scams, and honest businesses give you time to decide. As other questions in this section explain, there is no fee to get on a Section 8 waiting list, and no one can charge you a fee to renew Medicaid.

Warning signs: they ask for a fee up front. They tell you to pay with a gift card, a wire transfer (like Western Union or MoneyGram), a payment app or cryptocurrency. They rush you or say something bad will happen if you wait. They ask for personal details, like your Social Security number, bank account, EBT card PIN, or Medicaid or Medicare number.

What to do: stop and hang up, or don't answer the text or email. Don't click links. Call the office that runs the program yourself, using a number from your card, your letter or the agency's official website, such as your county Department of Social Services (DSS). Talk it over with someone you trust before you pay anyone.

If you already paid, call your bank, the gift card company or the wire company right away and ask them to stop or refund the payment. Then report the scam to the New York Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755 (ag.ny.gov) and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Reporting helps stop scammers, even if you did not lose money.

entries.q: How can I tell if a Section 8 waiting list website or an apartment ad is fake?
a: Fake websites copy the look of Section 8 sign-up pages. They often show up at the top of web search results and may use the words "Section 8" or an Equal Housing Opportunity logo. They take a fee or your personal information, and you never get on a real list. There is no fee to get on a Section 8 waiting list. Housing authorities do not call or email you to suggest you join a list, and they never ask you to wire money or pay with a prepaid card.

To get on a real list, contact your local housing authority yourself. Use HUD's list of local housing agencies, not a search ad. New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) also runs Section 8 through local offices in each county and takes applications for its open lists at its official MyHousing Portal, section8.hcr.ny.gov. HCR says it and its local offices will never ask a family to pay them directly for a deposit, rent or any other charge.

Rental ad scams: a fake landlord may offer low rent, say they can't show you the place, and rush you to pay an application fee, deposit or first month's rent by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency. Try to see the place in person, or have someone you trust see it, before you sign or pay. Search the address online. If the same home shows up with a different owner's name, or is listed for sale, it is a red flag. Don't send your Social Security number or a copy of your license until you know the landlord is real.
If you paid a scammer, report it to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to the New York Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755.

entries.q: How do thieves steal EBT benefits, and how do I spot a skimmer or a fake EBT text?
a: Thieves steal EBT benefits two main ways. Skimming: a fake cover (a "skimmer") is placed over a store's card reader or an ATM. It copies your card and PIN. Phishing: texts, emails or calls that look official and ask for your card number, PIN or login. New York State, county and EBT staff will never ask for your PIN. If anyone asks for it, assume it is a scam.

Check the card reader before you swipe. A skimmer may look loose, the wrong color, or a little different from the rest of the machine. It may cover lights or keypad numbers. The easiest check is to gently pull up on the reader; skimmers are flimsy and come right off. If something looks wrong, don't swipe. Tell the store manager, call the police, and tell your county DSS.

Protect your card with the free ebtEDGE app or ebtEDGE.com. Freeze your card when you are not using it, and unfreeze it at checkout. You can also block online and out-of-state purchases. Check your account often for charges you didn't make. Change your PIN often, such as once a month before your benefits come, and cover the keypad when you type it.

If your benefits were stolen, call EBT Customer Service at 1-888-328-6399 right away to cancel the card and get a new one. Stolen SNAP benefits can no longer be replaced, because federal permission to replace them ended December 20, 2024, and New York stopped taking SNAP claims on October 1, 2025. Stolen cash assistance may still be replaced, but only once each October-to-September year, and only if you apply within 30 days of finding out (see the question on SNAP renewals and stolen benefits).
New chip EBT cards, which are much harder to copy, are planned to start going out in early 2027. The state says cardholders will be told before their new card is sent.

entries.q: Someone called saying they are from National Grid or NYSEG and will shut off my power today unless I pay now. What do I do?
a: Hang up. This is a common scam. The caller ID may even say "National Grid" or show the company's real number; scammers can fake that (it is called "spoofing"). They often tell you to buy a prepaid card, like Green Dot or MoneyPak, and read them the numbers.

National Grid says it never demands payment with a prepaid debit card, never accepts those cards, and never threatens to shut you off right away. If it takes a payment by phone, you choose how to pay. NYSEG says it does not ask customers to buy debit cards to pay. Before a shutoff for an unpaid bill, a real utility must send you a written final notice and wait at least 15 days.

To check, call the utility yourself using the number on your bill or its official website, not a number the caller gave you. You can also ask the caller for the last five digits of your account number; a real National Grid worker will know it. Never give your account number, Social Security number or bank information to someone who calls you. If someone comes to your door, ask for a photo ID badge, and don't let them in without one.

If you paid a scammer, call your local police right away. You can also report it to the NYS Division of Consumer Protection at 1-800-697-1220 and to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If you really are behind on your bill, see the question on shutoff protections for your rights and for help paying.

entries.q: How do I spot a Medicare or Medicaid scam, like a call about a new card or free medical equipment?
a: Medicare will never call you to sell you anything or come to your home. It only calls in a few cases, like when you asked for a call back. Don't join a Medicare plan over the phone unless you made the call. Give your Medicare number only to your doctor or people you know should have it, like your insurance plan or HIICAP (New York's free Medicare counseling program).

Common Medicare scams: a caller, a booth at a health fair or someone at your door offers "free" medical care, such as a genetic test or cheek swab, and asks for your Medicare number. Then they bill Medicare for things you didn't need, or use your number for identity theft. If a test kit or equipment you didn't order comes in the mail, refuse it or send it back. Only a doctor you know and trust should order tests or services for you.

Medicaid scams: callers may say you will lose your Medicaid unless you pay to renew. No one can ever charge a fee to renew Medicaid, Child Health Plus or the Essential Plan. Government agencies will not threaten you, demand money, or ask for credit card information by text or phone call. If you're not sure, call your county DSS Medicaid office or NY State of Health at 1-855-355-5777.

Read your Medicare Summary Notice or plan statement and look for services you never got. To report Medicare fraud, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). New York's Senior Medicare Patrol, run by the StateWide Senior Action Council, gives free help spotting and reporting fraud at 1-800-333-4374. For free Medicare counseling, call HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501.

entries.q: Someone online or on a hotline wants to send me or my family member to rehab in another state. Can I trust them?
a: Be careful. Some people, called "patient brokers" or "body brokers," get paid by addiction treatment programs outside New York for every person they send there. New York's addiction agency says the care can cost more and be lower quality than care in New York.

New York passed a law in 2018 that bans paying or taking a fee in exchange for sending someone to a particular addiction treatment program. The law also protects people who refer someone in good faith without being paid.

To find real help, call or text New York's free, confidential 24/7 HOPEline: call 1-877-8-HOPENY (1-877-846-7369) or text HOPENY (467369). To check that a program is certified by the state, use the state Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) Provider and Program Search at findaddictiontreatment.ny.gov.
If someone has approached you, or you think a referral was fraud, report it to OASAS at 1-800-553-5790, or use the contact on the OASAS Stop Treatment Fraud page (oasas.ny.gov).

entries.q: A caller says they are from Social Security or the IRS and I will be arrested or lose my benefits. Is it real?
a: No. These are some of the most common scams. The caller may use a real employee's name, fake the caller ID, or send a picture of a badge. They may say your Social Security number will be suspended, that you owe money, or that you must move your money to a "safe" account. They tell you to pay with gift cards, prepaid debit cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, gold or cash. Real agencies don't do this.

The IRS normally contacts you first by mail. IRS impostors threaten arrest, demand payment right now, often by gift card, prepaid card or wire transfer, and don't let you question or appeal what you owe. The real IRS doesn't work that way.

What to do: hang up or ignore the message. Don't click links. If you want to check, call Social Security or the IRS yourself at a number from their official website or from a letter you got. Report Social Security scams to the Social Security Office of the Inspector General at oig.ssa.gov/report. For help reporting in another language, call the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) at 1-877-382-4357 and press 3.

If you gave a scammer money or personal information, it is not your fault. Call your local police. Go to IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan, and ask the credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) to put a fraud alert on your credit report. Creating your own my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount can help stop someone else from changing your address or direct deposit.

entries.q: A company says it can wipe out my debt or fix my credit fast. Is it safe?
a: Be very careful. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says no one can legally remove information from your credit report if it is correct and current. It is illegal for credit repair companies to lie about what they can do or to charge you before they help you. If a company asks for money first, or offers a "new credit identity," it is a scam, and using a number that isn't yours to get credit can get you in legal trouble.

Debt settlement companies say they can get your creditors to take less than you owe. This is risky. They often tell you to stop paying your bills, which can lead to more late fees, calls from debt collectors and a lower credit score. By law, a debt settlement company can't collect its fee until it actually settles a debt.

You can do a lot for free. Call the people you owe and ask for a payment plan you can afford. You can check your credit reports for free at AnnualCreditReport.com, and disputing mistakes on your report is free. For mortgage or housing trouble, a HUD-approved housing counselor can help; foreclosure counseling is free, and agencies must waive fees you can't afford. Call 1-800-569-4287 to find one.

Before you sign up with any company, check it with the New York Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755. If you are being sued or a debt collector is calling, see the question on debt collectors. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Should I call 988, 911, or a mobile crisis team?
a: Call 911 if someone is in physical danger right now. Examples are a suicide attempt in progress, a suspected overdose, or a medical emergency like chest pain or trouble breathing. 911 sends police, an ambulance or fire crews.

Call or text 988, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, for a mental health, suicide or substance use crisis when no one is in immediate physical danger. You can also chat at 988lifeline.org. It is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. You can reach out for yourself or for someone you are worried about.

When you call 988, a recording first offers choices: press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line, press 2 for Spanish, or stay on the line for a local crisis center. A trained counselor answers, listens, helps you stay safe, and shares resources. Most calls are handled on the phone. Counselors contact 911 only in a small share of calls, when a life is at risk right now, and often with the caller's agreement.

A mobile crisis team is a small team of trained staff, which may include a peer (someone with lived experience), who come to you at home or another place in the community. It is voluntary and aims to calm the crisis where you are and avoid an emergency room or hospital stay when possible. In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, Northern Rivers Family of Services runs mobile crisis teams for adults, children and teens. Find the number in the Crisis Help category of this directory. If the team is not available, call 988, or 911 in an emergency.

entries.q: What happens at a psychiatric emergency room, and what are my rights?
a: In a mental health crisis, a hospital emergency room doctor will examine you and decide what care you need. Some larger hospitals have a CPEP (Comprehensive Psychiatric Emergency Program), a 24-hour crisis center inside the hospital. A CPEP can keep someone in an observation bed for up to 72 hours, which often avoids a longer hospital stay.

Voluntary care means you agree to it. You sign a form asking to be admitted. If you want to leave, tell the hospital in writing. The hospital must then let you go promptly, unless the director thinks you need involuntary care. In that case, the hospital has 72 hours to either let you go or ask a court for an order to keep you.

Involuntary care (sometimes called a hold) happens without your agreement. Under New York's Mental Hygiene Law, it is allowed only when a mental illness is likely to cause serious harm. That means a danger to yourself or others, or being unable or unwilling, because of the illness, to meet your own basic needs like food, clothing, shelter, medical care or safety. Voluntary care should be tried first whenever possible. In an emergency admission, a psychiatrist must confirm the need within 48 hours, and the stay can last up to 15 days. Keeping someone longer takes more doctor reviews, and you or someone acting for you can ask for a court hearing.

You have rights. You must get a written notice of your legal status and rights. You can have visitors, contact people outside the hospital, talk with a lawyer, and help make your treatment plan. Mental Hygiene Legal Service (MHLS) is a free, independent court agency. MHLS can answer your or your family's legal questions and represent you in court. Ask any staff member to connect you.

Family and friends can help. A patient age 16 or older can ask a relative or close friend to take part in treatment planning. Before discharge, the hospital must help plan your care after you leave. For insurance problems with mental health or addiction care, the state's CHAMP help line is 888-614-5400. This is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact MHLS or a free legal aid office.

entries.q: Where can I get free Narcan (naloxone), and will I get in trouble for calling 911 during an overdose?
a: Naloxone (brand name Narcan) is a medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose. Opioids include heroin, fentanyl and many prescription pain pills. Signs of an overdose: the person can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or not at all, makes gurgling sounds, or has blue or gray lips. Call 911 right away.

Ways to get naloxone in New York: Narcan nasal spray is sold over the counter, with no prescription. Pharmacies in New York can also give naloxone without a prescription from your own doctor. If you have insurance with drug coverage, the state's N-CAP program can lower or cover the copay at participating pharmacies. Registered community overdose prevention programs give free naloxone kits and free training. OASAS (the state Office of Addiction Services and Supports) also mails free naloxone through an online order form; it takes about two weeks to arrive.

Fentanyl test strips check a drug for fentanyl, a very strong opioid that is often mixed into other drugs. You can order them free through the same OASAS form or get them from a local overdose prevention program.

New York's 911 Good Samaritan Law protects people of any age who call 911 for an overdose, and the person who overdosed. You can't be charged for having drugs (less than 8 ounces), having marijuana, having drug equipment, sharing drugs, or underage drinking. It does not protect against selling drugs, open warrants, or probation or parole violations. Questions: call 1-800-692-8528.

entries.q: How can I find out what's in my drugs (test strips and drug checking)?
a: Street drugs often contain things people don't expect, like fentanyl (a very strong opioid) or xylazine ("tranq", an animal sedative that slows breathing and can cause bad wounds). Checking first can help prevent an overdose.

Test strips at home: fentanyl and xylazine test strips are small paper strips that show whether a drug contains fentanyl or xylazine. They only show yes or no, and a negative result does not prove a drug is safe. Order them free by mail from New York State (OASAS), or call MATTERS at (765) 628-8377. Mail orders take about two weeks. Follow the instructions that come with them.

Drug checking: New York State runs free, confidential drug checking at some harm reduction programs. Staff test a tiny amount, about the size of a match head, with a lab machine that can find several drugs and cutting agents at once. The state Health Department keeps the current list of sites on its Drug Checking web page. Sites change, so call before you go. Local harm reduction programs in the Substance Use and Recovery category can tell you what is available near you.

No test is perfect. Different parts of the same batch can hold different amounts, so a test only tells you about the part that was tested. Carry naloxone (Narcan), try not to use alone, and start with a small amount. Naloxone does not reverse xylazine, but still give it and call 911 for any overdose. If you do use alone, the Never Use Alone line, (800) 484-3731, stays on the phone and sends help if you stop responding.

entries.q: How do I start medicine for opioid addiction (buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone)?
a: Medicine is the standard treatment for opioid use disorder (opioid addiction). There are three medicines: buprenorphine (often called Suboxone or "bupe"), methadone, and a monthly naltrexone shot (Vivitrol). Buprenorphine comes as a film or tablet you take every day, or as a shot given once a week or once a month (brands Sublocade and Brixadi) by a health care provider. It eases withdrawal and cravings, and it helps protect against overdose if someone uses opioids again.

Buprenorphine can be prescribed in many places, including a regular doctor's office or clinic, and filled at a local pharmacy. The special "X-waiver" that prescribers used to need was removed by federal law at the end of 2022. Now any prescriber with the right DEA registration can prescribe it, and there is no limit on how many patients they treat.

Methadone for addiction can only be given at a certified opioid treatment program (OTP), sometimes called a methadone clinic. There are fewer of these programs in rural areas, so you may need to travel. To find one with openings, call the HOPEline or search FindTreatment.gov. You take your dose at the program at first. Once you are stable, you may be allowed to take some doses home. The naltrexone shot can be given in a medical office, but opioids must be fully out of your body first.

Cost: New York Medicaid covers all three. The state's Medicaid drug list covers its preferred buprenorphine and naltrexone products without prior approval. If you have no insurance or not enough coverage, the state's Buprenorphine Assistance Program (BUPE-AP) can pay for buprenorphine. Call 1-800-542-2437 to check if you qualify.

To start, ask your doctor, or call the NY HOPEline (1-877-846-7369, or text 467369) to find treatment near you. You can also search FindTreatment.gov, or see the Substance Use and Recovery category in this directory. Call a program first to ask which medicines it offers and whether it has openings.

entries.q: What is a peer advocate or recovery coach, and how do I find one?
a: A peer is someone who has lived through a similar struggle, like addiction or a mental health condition, and is trained to support others. Peers are not therapists. They use their own experience to listen, give hope, and help you find your way through services.

For addiction, New York has Certified Recovery Peer Advocates (CRPAs), sometimes called recovery coaches. They can help you get into treatment, support you after a hospital stay or jail, teach about different paths to recovery, go with you to medical appointments, connect you to recovery groups, and help you apply for benefits. They work in treatment programs, hospital emergency rooms, community programs and courts.

For mental health, New York Certified Peer Specialists are in recovery from a mental health condition themselves. Family Peer Advocates are parents or caregivers who have raised a child with emotional or behavioral needs, and they help other families. Youth Peer Advocates are young adults with lived experience who help young people.

To find one, ask your treatment program, clinic or hospital if they have peer staff. Recovery community centers offer free, drug- and alcohol-free places for peer support, groups and activities. entries.q: What is SPOA (Single Point of Access)?
a: SPOA (Single Point of Access) is the county process for referrals to high-intensity mental health services, such as intensive or supportive case management, residential (housing) programs, and Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) teams. The process is a little different in each county.

In Warren and Washington Counties, the Office of Community Services for Warren and Washington Counties runs SPOA. Adults must be over 18, have a serious mental illness, and need services because the illness makes it very hard to function in the community. Children and youth with a serious emotional disturbance have their own SPOA committee.
There, a referral needs the SPOA application, a signed release of information, and a psychosocial or psychiatric assessment. Residential programs need a few more forms.
For ACT, a referral can come from the person, a family member, a mental health agency, a hospital, police or a court.

In Saratoga County, SPOA is run by Saratoga County Mental Health and Addiction Services, for both adults and children. Fill out the adult or youth SPOA referral form from the county website and send it with a signed release of information. Questions: call (518) 584-9030. Both SPOA offices are listed in this directory under Case Management.

entries.q: How does someone get OPWDD services (the Front Door)?
a: OPWDD (Office for People With Developmental Disabilities) serves people with developmental disabilities, such as intellectual disability, autism, cerebral palsy, epilepsy or a similar condition. Under state law, the disability must have started before age 22, be expected to last, and make daily life much harder.

The "Front Door" is how OPWDD connects you to services. Step 1: call the OPWDD Infoline at 866-946-9733, tell them your county, and ask to be transferred to your local Front Door office. Step 2: OPWDD decides if you are eligible. Step 3: if you are, you start planning services with Front Door staff.

Eligibility usually needs a psychological report with IQ testing and an adaptive behavior assessment (for conditions other than intellectual disability, a medical or specialist report instead), a general medical report from the past 12 months, and a history showing the disability began before age 22. A Care Coordination Organization (CCO) can help you through the process.

Being found eligible does not by itself give you most services. Many services also need Medicaid. If you are found not eligible, you can meet with staff about the decision and ask for another review. If you asked for Medicaid-funded services, you can also ask for a Medicaid fair hearing. Your written notice explains your options.

entries.q: What is the difference between Early Intervention and CPSE?
a: Early Intervention (EI) is for babies and toddlers under age 3 who have a disability or a developmental delay. It is run by the state Department of Health and your county. Services like speech, physical and occupational therapy can happen at home, at child care, or wherever your child spends the day. There is no cost to families.

To refer a child to EI, call your county Early Intervention program. The Growing Up Healthy Hotline, 1-800-522-5006 (weekdays, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.), can give you the number. The county EI offices are also listed in this directory.

CPSE (Committee on Preschool Special Education) is for children ages 3 to 5. It is part of your school district. If a child may need special education, a parent or professional can refer the child in writing to the chairperson of the district's CPSE. The evaluation is at no cost to the family.

If your child is in EI, the EI service coordinator helps you plan the move to CPSE. A transition plan should be made at least three months before the child's third birthday. The CPSE should decide eligibility by the third birthday so services can continue. Parents of eligible children can choose to move to preschool special education or stay in EI until the child is no longer age-eligible for EI.

entries.q: My school-age child is struggling. What is the difference between an IEP and a 504 plan?
a: An IEP (Individualized Education Program) is a written plan for a student with a disability who needs special education. It sets goals and lists services, such as special classes or therapy. In New York, each school district's Committee on Special Education (CSE) decides who qualifies and writes the IEP for school-age students (ages 5 to 21). For younger children, see our entry on Early Intervention and CPSE.

A 504 plan comes from a federal civil rights law called Section 504. It covers students with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, such as learning, reading or concentrating. The plan lists supports and changes (called accommodations) so the student can learn alongside other students. A student does not have to be failing to qualify. A school's Section 504 team, usually not the CSE, handles 504 plans.

To ask for a special education evaluation, write a letter to the CSE chairperson or your child's principal. Say you think your child may have a disability and ask for an initial evaluation. Date it and keep a copy. The district must ask for your written consent. The evaluation is free and must be done within 60 calendar days after the district gets your consent.

Parents have rights. You get a copy of the evaluation report. If you disagree with it, you can ask for an independent evaluation (IEE) at the district's cost. You can also ask for free mediation or an impartial hearing. State-funded Family and Community Engagement (FACE) Centers help parents understand the process. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Can my child go to Head Start or free pre-K?
a: Head Start is a free federal program that helps young children get ready for school. Early Head Start serves pregnant women and children from birth to age 3. Head Start preschool serves children ages 3 to 5. All programs welcome children with disabilities.

Who qualifies for Head Start: families with income at or below the federal poverty guidelines. Children also qualify no matter the income if they are in foster care, are homeless, or the family gets TANF (cash assistance), SSI or SNAP (food stamps). Pregnant women may qualify for Early Head Start. Some programs can also take a small number of families with higher incomes, so it is worth asking.

How to apply: contact your local program. Find it in the Pregnancy and Young Children category of this directory or with the Head Start Center Locator on headstart.gov. The program will check if your child qualifies, give you the forms, and tell you what papers to bring. If there is no space, ask to join the waiting list. For help finding a program, call 1-866-763-6481 (weekdays, noon to 6 p.m.).

Universal pre-K (UPK) is free pre-kindergarten through public school districts, sometimes held at child care centers. Children who live in the district can go the school year they turn 4, usually on or before December 1 (some districts use a different date). There is no income test. Call your school district to ask when registration starts. If there are more children than seats, the district holds a lottery. Some districts also have pre-K for 3-year-olds.

Pre-K is growing. Under the 2026-27 state budget, every district can get state money for pre-K. By the 2028-29 school year, districts must offer a full-day pre-K seat to every eligible 4-year-old whose family asks for one.

entries.q: After someone is found eligible for OPWDD, what happens next?
a: After OPWDD finds someone eligible, Front Door staff give you information about the Care Coordination Organizations (CCOs) in your area. A CCO is an agency that provides a care manager. You choose the CCO, and the CCO helps you enroll.

You also choose a type of care management. Health Home Care Management is the full option. A care manager helps you get disability services and also coordinates medical, dental and mental health care, and links you to housing, jobs and family supports. Basic HCBS Plan Support is a very small option. It keeps your plan up to date but does not coordinate health or mental health care, and you will have less contact with your care manager.

Your care manager works with you to write your Life Plan. The Life Plan is built around your goals and needs. It covers your disability supports and your other services, like medical, dental and mental health care. It is updated when your needs change.

Most OPWDD services need Medicaid, including care coordination and HCBS waiver services (home and community-based services such as respite, day programs, supported employment and residential care). Front Door staff or a CCO can help you apply for Medicaid.

The CCO does not approve or cut services. OPWDD's regional office does that. If you are not happy, you can ask for a different care manager, change your level of care management, or switch to another CCO in your region.

entries.q: Who pays for rehab, home health care, a nursing home or assisted living?
a: Medicare pays for short-term skilled care, not long-term help with daily living. Skilled care is care from nurses or therapists, like wound care or physical therapy after a hospital stay. Help with bathing, dressing and eating is called custodial care, and Medicare does not pay for long-term care like that.

Rehab in a nursing home: after an inpatient hospital stay of at least 3 days in a row, Original Medicare can pay for a skilled nursing facility (SNF) for up to 100 days in each benefit period, if you need daily skilled care. Time under observation does not count toward the 3 days. In 2026, you pay $0 for days 1 to 20 (after the $1,736 Part A deductible, which you usually already paid for the hospital stay), $217 a day for days 21 to 100, and all costs after day 100. These amounts change each January. You usually must enter the SNF within 30 days of leaving the hospital. See the question on observation status.

Home health care: Medicare pays the full cost of part-time skilled nursing and therapy at home if you are homebound and a doctor or certain other providers, like a nurse practitioner, confirm you need it. (You may pay 20% for medical equipment.) It does not pay for 24-hour care, meals, cleaning, or personal care when that is the only help you need.

Long-term care: Medicaid can pay for long-term care for people who qualify, at home (see the MLTC and CDPAP questions) or in a nursing home. Apply at your county Department of Social Services. Otherwise, people pay on their own or with private long-term care insurance.

Assisted living: Medicare does not pay for it. New York's Assisted Living Program (ALP) is for people who would otherwise need a nursing home but don't need constant nursing care. Both Medicaid members and people paying privately can use it. An ALP provides room, meals, personal care, nursing and therapy. Contact an ALP directly; Medicaid members also need approval from their county DSS. For free help sorting out your options, call NY Connects or your county Office for the Aging (see the "Where do I start?" question).

entries.q: What does the Office for the Aging do, and who can use it?
a: Each county has an Office for the Aging. It helps people age 60 and older stay safe and independent at home. Many services, like meals, have no income limit. Some ask for a voluntary donation, and some in-home help uses a sliding scale (the cost depends on income).

Local offices: Warren County is served by the Warren/Hamilton Counties Office for the Aging in Lake George. Washington County has the Office for Aging and Disabilities Resource Center in Fort Edward. In Saratoga County, the office is called the Department of Aging and Youth Services, in Ballston Spa. NY Connects gives free, unbiased help with long-term care to older adults and to people of any age with a disability. Your county office can connect you, or call NY Connects statewide at 1-800-342-9871.

Home-delivered meals (often called Meals on Wheels) go to people 60 and older who are homebound and can't make their own meals. A spouse may get meals too. Group meals at senior dining sites are open to anyone 60 or older and their spouse. A donation is suggested but not required.

EISEP (Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program) gives non-medical help at home, like housekeeping, shopping, bathing and dressing, plus a case manager. It is for people 60 and older who need help with daily tasks, can stay safely at home, and are not eligible for the same help through Medicaid. You may be asked to share the cost based on income, and there may be a waiting list.

Offices also offer HIICAP Medicare counseling, caregiver support and respite (a break for caregivers), help with benefit applications, and rides for older adults. Call your county office to ask what is offered where you live.

entries.q: What is Adult Protective Services (APS), and what happens after a report?
a: Adult Protective Services (APS) helps adults age 18 and older who live in the community and, because of a physical or mental impairment, can't protect themselves from abuse, neglect or financial exploitation (someone misusing their money or property). It is for people who have no one willing and able to help them responsibly. APS is run by each county's Department of Social Services (DSS).

Anyone can make a report, and you can stay anonymous. Call your county DSS and ask for Adult Protective Services, or call the statewide line at 1-844-697-3505 on weekdays. If someone is in danger right now, call 911.

After a report, APS visits the person's home within three working days, or within 24 hours if the situation is life-threatening. A caseworker looks at the risks and offers help. Help can include counseling, medical or mental health checks, help applying for benefits, help managing money, homemaker services, or finding a safer place to live. In serious cases, APS can ask a court for protective orders or a guardian.

An adult who has mental capacity (can understand the risks and make their own choices) has the right to refuse help, even if others disagree. APS will keep offering help and try to convince the person to accept it. If there are questions about the person's capacity, APS will seek a mental health evaluation to decide if a court should step in.

entries.q: What is the difference between hospice and palliative care?
a: Palliative care is extra support for people with a serious illness, at any age and any stage. A team works to ease pain, other symptoms and stress. You can keep getting treatment to cure or control your illness at the same time. You can ask your doctor about a palliative care referral.

Hospice is a type of palliative care for people near the end of life. For Medicare, your doctor and the hospice doctor must certify that you are expected to live 6 months or less if the illness runs its usual course. Care focuses on comfort instead of a cure. Hospice is usually given at home, or in a nursing home or assisted living. It also supports the family, including grief counseling for about a year after a death.

Choosing hospice does not mean giving up all care. Medicare still covers health problems that are not related to the terminal illness. You can keep seeing your regular doctor. You can stop hospice at any time and go back to treatment for your illness, and you can sign up for hospice again later if you qualify.

Who pays: Medicare Part A covers hospice. You pay nothing for hospice care, except up to $5 per prescription for pain and symptom drugs and a small share (5%) for short inpatient respite stays. Medicare's hospice benefit does not pay room and board in a nursing home. New York Medicaid also covers hospice. Palliative care is billed in different ways, so ask a social worker or your health plan what is covered.

New York law requires doctors and nurse practitioners to offer information about palliative care and end-of-life options to patients with a terminal illness (one expected to cause death within 6 months). You can always ask for it yourself. See the Hospice and Caregiver Support category in this directory.

entries.q: I'm a family caregiver and I need a break. What help is there?
a: Respite means short-term care for your loved one so you can rest, work, or take care of yourself. It can happen at home, when a worker comes in, or outside the home, such as at an adult day program, a senior center, or a short stay in a nursing home or assisted living.

Your county Office for the Aging runs caregiver programs. Through the National Family Caregiver Support Program, they can offer information, counseling, support groups, training and respite. You may qualify if you are an adult caring for someone 60 or older, or for someone of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. Relatives 55 or older who are raising a child, or caring for an adult relative age 18 to 59 with a disability, may also qualify.

The State Respite Program and EISEP (in-home help for people 60 and older) can also provide respite. In our three counties, the State Respite Program is run by Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Albany. To ask, call your county Office for the Aging or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871.

For memory loss or dementia, the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline is free: 1-800-272-3900. Staff can help with caregiver stress, behavior changes, safety, care planning, respite, and finding local programs. Interpreters are available in more than 200 languages.
If the person has Medicaid, CDPAP may pay a family member to give care (see our CDPAP entry). See the Hospice and Caregiver Support category in this directory for local help.

entries.q: I don't drive. How can I get around in Warren, Washington or Saratoga County?
a: If you have Medicaid, you can get free rides to medical appointments. See our entry on Medicaid rides. For other trips, here are the main options.

CDTA buses: CDTA (Capital District Transportation Authority) runs public buses in the Glens Falls area and in parts of Saratoga County. Glens Falls routes reach places like Hudson Falls, Fort Edward, South Glens Falls and Moreau. Glens Falls routes and times changed in August 2026 and can change again, so check cdta.org or call CDTA at (518) 482-8822.

Half fare: People 65 and older, people with a disability, and honorably discharged veterans can ride CDTA buses for half fare all day. You need a CDTA half-fare photo ID card. Bring a photo ID showing your age; proof of disability such as a Medicare card, recent SSI or SSDI papers, or a VA disability letter; or veteran papers such as a DD-214.

You must apply first; the application needs a form from your medical provider and an in-person assessment. Book up to 7 days ahead, and no later than 4 p.m. the day before. Office for the Aging rides: Each county Office for the Aging offers or arranges some rides for people 60 and older, often for medical visits and shopping, but what is offered differs by county and town. In Washington County, rides for people 60 and older who don't have Medicaid are arranged through LEAP, and eligible people 60 and older with no other way to travel may get free GoGoGrandparent rides (using Uber or Lyft) while funding lasts. You must register with the Office for Aging first. Rural Washington County has very little public transit: CDTA buses there mainly serve the Hudson Falls and Fort Edward area. entries.q: What is a health care proxy, and what is a MOLST?
a: A health care proxy is a form where you name a health care agent: a person you trust to make medical decisions for you if you can no longer make them. The state says everyone over 18 should have one. You can download the free New York Health Care Proxy form from the Department of Health.

You don't need a lawyer or a notary. Sign it in front of two adult witnesses; the person you name as your agent can't be a witness. Talk with your agent about what matters to you. Give copies to your agent, your doctor and your family, and keep one in your wallet.

A MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is different. It is a medical order form signed by a doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, for people with serious health conditions. It records choices like whether to have CPR or a breathing tube.

In New York, the MOLST is the only approved form that can hold both a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) and a do-not-intubate (DNI) order outside the hospital. It travels with the patient to other care settings.

entries.q: How do I get a New York State ID card?
a: Anyone of any age with lawful status in the U.S. can get a New York non-driver ID card. You must apply in person at a DMV office. You get a temporary paper document that day, and the card comes in the mail.

Bring a completed application (form MV-44), the fee, and proofs of identity. DMV uses a point system: your proofs of name must add up to at least 6 points. You must also give your Social Security number (a card is not always needed), or show that you never got one. You can't hold a New York driver license and a non-driver ID at the same time.

If you are under 21, a parent or guardian can vouch for your identity by signing form MV-45 at the DMV and showing their own proof of identity. DMV has other forms for some people who lack papers, such as young people who are homeless (MV-45B).

The fee is small, and it is lower or free for some people, such as those 62 and older, on SSI, or on public assistance; bring proof. Check the DMV's document list before you go, because some documents do not count for a REAL ID or Enhanced ID.
